title: App requests and toolkit types
text: App Requests and Toolkits are two separate controls over what members can reach: which catalog applications a project is allowed to use, and which toolkit types exist on the deployment at all. Decide an app request A member who opens the application catalog and requests access to something their project is not configured for creates a row here — separate from the agent/skill publishing review, which is a different mechanism entirely. The queue lists pending requests with who asked and for what. Both record your decision and notify the requester in the same transaction. Approving a request records the decision and tells the requester — it does not itself grant anything. Nothing in the platform reads an approved row and automatically unlocks a capability; whether the requested application actually becomes usable depends on whether its toolkit type is enabled for that project, below. Control which toolkit types are offered Open Toolkits . This decides, per toolkit type, whether it is enabled, disabled, or restricted to named projects — always with a reason and a recorded decider. The table lists every catalogue type with its current availability and a worker support indicator. Choose enabled, disabled, or restricted; a restricted type also lists which projects can use it. A reason is required for every choice except reverting to the default. This page does not add a new toolkit type. A pre built MCP server becomes a type through Configuration's MCP Servers section, and an external provider's toolkits would arrive through Service Descriptors — a third registration path here would be a third thing to keep synchronized. The worker column is advisory: it reports whether the toolkit type is known to run on the deployment's configured worker, not whether the type is disallowed. Elitea can run its agent runtime on either a Rust worker (Helm's default) or a Python worker (compose's default), and their toolkit coverage differs: Rust worker default hides 17 toolkit types that only run on the Python worker (for example Jira, Confluence, GitHub, Bitbucket, and several others) — tracked in 865. Python worker default fails to import 4 toolkit types that only run on the Rust worker (Google Places, Rally, ServiceNow, and Slack) — tracked in 869. Check which worker your deployment runs before assuming a type's tile will actually work.

title: Audit trail
text: Audit Trail is a read only view over what happened on the deployment — there is nothing to edit or configure here. Use it to answer "who did this, and when," whether you are investigating an incident, confirming a change actually landed, or checking whether a scheduled job ran. Review activity User events are actions a person took; System events are platform generated (for example a scheduled job firing). Each has its own tab. Narrow by date range (with quick presets like 30 minutes, today, yesterday, 7 days, or 30 days, plus an explicit From/To), event type, project, user, or errors only. A calendar style heatmap shows activity density over time, so a spike is visible before you drill into individual events. Traces and spans A second view mode, alongside events, shows execution traces and their individual spans — each row names the action and, when there is one, the tool or model that ran it. Spans can be filtered by duration band (under 10 ms, up to over 10 seconds), which is the fastest way to find what is running slowly across the deployment rather than one conversation at a time. Investigate one person From the Users page's row menu, the activity drawer filters this same audit data to one account — useful when investigating a specific person's actions rather than browsing the whole trail. See Users and roles. This page has no write path of any kind. An audit trail the product could edit would not be one. Audit Trail records what happened; it does not enforce anything. If you are looking for the controls that decide who can do what in the first place, see Users and roles.

title: Authentication
text: Authentication lives under Configuration › Authentication in the admin console. It covers how people sign in (OIDC or SAML) and how an identity provider's groups map onto project membership (SCIM). Configure an identity provider The list shows any providers already configured, one live per protocol. Choose OpenID Connect or SAML 2.0 . Issuer URL (a .well known/openid configuration URL is accepted and reduced to its issuer), Client ID, client secret, redirect URI, scopes, and whether e mail verification is required. Identity provider entity ID, SSO URL, single logout URL, and certificate(s); this service's own entity ID and ACS URL; name ID format; the e mail and name attribute mappings; whether to sign AuthnRequests; the service provider certificate; and clock skew tolerance. Turning a provider on retires any other provider of the same protocol — only one live OIDC and one live SAML definition can exist at a time, because each protocol is served on one route. A stored secret is never shown in the clear — the field renders a mask, and there is no "reveal" control. To change it, enter a new value; leaving it blank keeps the existing one. Deleting a provider also deletes its stored secret, which cannot be recovered. To stop using a provider for new logins without losing its configuration, turn off "use this provider for logins" instead of deleting it. Bind SCIM groups to a project role SCIM lets an identity provider push its directory — creating and deactivating accounts as people join and leave — rather than only federating logins. The SCIM endpoint is /api/v2/scim/v2 , authenticated with a personal access token; configuring it in your identity provider is outside Elitea's UI. What the admin console does provide is the group to role mapping, beneath the identity provider list: Name the SCIM group exactly as your identity provider sends it, and choose the project and role it grants. A member the group granted the role to loses it when they leave the group. A member who already held that role independently keeps it — the identity provider is authoritative only over what it granted, not over everything it happens to find. A SCIM group with no binding is refused by name; it never creates a project on its own, and it never guesses a role.

title: Branding
text: Branding is a runtime setting, not a build step: changes reach every user on their next page load, with no rebuild or restart required. The brand pack you edit here is what the platform serves to every client on the deployment — there is no per project or per user brand. Edit the brand pack The form is grouped into identity, color/type/shape, assets, and font faces. Every field can inherit from the platform default instead of being set explicitly, and the form says what it would inherit and from where. Logos and other assets are uploaded directly; self hosted font faces are declared here rather than linked externally. A sample surface renders in both light and dark under a theme built from your current draft, including the derived color swatches and a text on primary contrast check. The check is a warning only — it does not block saving. The merged pack becomes what every user's next page load receives. Import, export, and restore a package Download the current brand as a package. Uploading a package runs a dry run first, so you see what would change before committing it. Kept versions can be restored from the package panel. An unsaved draft is respected by the import and restore controls — neither silently discards edits you have not saved yet. What is inherited by default Every branding field defaults to the platform's own look unless you override it. This means a fresh deployment already looks complete without any editing here — Branding is where you replace that default with your organization's identity, one field at a time, not something you must fully populate before it is usable.

title: Budgets and LLM governance
text: Budgets and LLM Governance are two separate admin pages that both shape how the LLM gateway treats a request. Set spend limits Open Budgets . Each row is a project or a project member with a spend ceiling. Search, then open its budget dialog. Choose a monthly limit, or mark it unlimited. The gateway bills on the calendar month; no other period is enforced. Choose whether the gateway fails open (allows calls through) or fails closed (refuses calls) if it cannot reach its budget counter, or inherit the platform default. Open the members drawer to set a spend ceiling for an individual project member, on top of the project ceiling. A budget stored here is only enforced if the LLM gateway is configured with GATEWAY NATS URL . Without it, every number on this page round trips and saves, but no call is ever refused for exceeding it. The page shows a warning only when the gateway itself reports enforcement is off — never from silence. Not available yet: the budget and usage numbers here are per (project, member, period) only — there is no per agent or per tool cost breakdown. Spend cannot be attributed to which agent or which tool caused it (tracked in 875). Author LLM governance rules Open LLM Governance . Each row is a scoped rule the gateway reads and enforces on the /llm path: budgets, rate limits, model and MCP server allowlists, credential rate policy, and CEL based routing rules. Choose the scope it applies to (provider, model, or project) and the rule fields for that scope. A saved definition does not take effect immediately — the gateway polls this table on a refresh interval (30 seconds by default) rather than reloading on every write, so a replica that missed an event still converges. A saved rule can still be unenforceable: it may fail to load, or load and match nothing it could ever apply to. The gateway's own status report (surfaced on the LLM proxy Status tab) names any rule it rejected — a save here is not proof the rule is in force.

title: Features and configuration
text: Features and Configuration are two admin pages that share one mechanism: a list of sections, each either editable here or pointing you to where it actually lives. A section that this deployment cannot serve says so, with a reason, instead of rendering a form that saves into nothing. Features Whether Elitea exposes an MCP server at all, and whether MCP servers show in the main navigation. Block agent publishing platform wide, restrict it to named projects, and set the categories offered. The same three controls, for skills. Turn on the project Analytics tab (Settings › Analytics). The links shown on the in app Help Center page. Enable the assistant, and set which project and agent answer it. Turn voice input and text to speech on, or keep the controls visible but disabled. From the list on the left. Only changed fields are sent; Discard reverts unsaved edits. Configuration Configuration holds the sections Features does not: some editable directly here, some pointing to a dedicated page. Blocked toolkit types (a blocked type cannot be listed or created, and is stripped from every agent before it runs — existing toolkits of that type stay visible so an administrator can review and delete them, but stop working); blocked individual tools within an otherwise allowed toolkit; tools that require the user to authorize each call ("sensitive action" tools, matched per toolkit or with for every toolkit); the company name and message template shown in that authorization dialog. A dismissible banner shown across the app, with its own icon, style, and message. Turns on maintenance mode: every caller without administration access gets a 503 and the splash screen, with its own title, message, and optional HTML. The admin console and authentication routes stay reachable so the window is reversible from inside itself. The outbound mail relay: SMTP host, port, TLS mode, credentials, from/reply to addresses, and the public base URL used in links the platform sends. Environment variables ( SMTP HOST and its siblings) provide a second layer underneath these rows; a row set here wins over the environment field by field. These sections carry credentials or need a row editor shape a flat form cannot express, so each is a page of its own: see Authentication, LLM proxy, and Branding. MCP Servers configures the pre built MCP server catalogue; see the MCP integration guides for what that catalogue offers. Stays unavailable on this page specifically, because a governance corpus is a list of scoped rules rather than one value document. See Budgets and LLM governance. A registry for external provider integrations. This deployment publishes none, so the page reports that rather than showing an empty grid. Configuration's "Advanced", "Observability", "Runtime", and "Admin Panel" sections from the legacy admin UI have no counterpart here — their fields addressed process environment variables and mounted files that no form could ever write, so they were removed rather than kept as permanently unavailable placeholders.

title: LLM proxy
text: The LLM Proxy screen lives under Configuration › LLM Proxy in the admin console. It is the platform wide control over the LLM gateway that sits in front of every model call, organized into six tabs. Whether the gateway is reachable, and whether rate limits and budgets are actually enforceable right now. The platform model catalogue and its per project grants. Deployment wide spend by provider and model. A per request log of every call the gateway served. Publish a provider credential once for the whole platform. The default soft alert threshold for budget warnings. Publish a provider platform wide Normally an AI provider credential belongs to one project. Providers & models lets you publish one from the public project instead, so every project can use it without configuring its own copy. Existing platform providers are listed with a status ok indicator — the gateway only ever dispatches to a provider whose endpoint and key resolve, so a row reporting status ok = false is stored and listed but silently never used. Same provider types as a project credential (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, EPAM DIAL, Anthropic, Ollama, Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, vLLM). A row imported from an older deployment can still hold its key as plain text rather than sealed in the vault. The panel flags this as sealed: false without ever displaying the value; re saving the credential through this screen seals it. Grant a platform model to specific projects Under Models , each platform model carries a share scope: All projects — every project on the deployment can use it (the default for any model saved before this control existed). No project — stored and listed, but offered nowhere. Selected projects — offered only to the team projects you pick. Personal projects are not offered here individually — granting to one would be a grant to a single person, which this screen does not do. Choose the share scope, and for Selected projects , search and pick which team projects. The model becomes available (or unavailable) to the chosen projects' model pickers. credential resolves = false on a model means it names a provider this platform does not currently publish (or none). That, like status ok = false , means the model is stored and listed but never actually served — this screen is where you see why. Read status, usage, logs, and alerts Reports what the gateway currently holds, not what was last saved — a governance rule can be rejected at load, or load but match nothing, and neither looks different from the authoring side. If the gateway is unreachable, the panel says so rather than showing stale numbers as if they were live. Reads the per request billing ledger, deployment wide, broken down by provider and model. This is a report, not a control — nothing here enforces a budget; that happens on Budgets and governance. Reads every request the gateway served, including ones a billing based Usage report would miss entirely — refused by a budget, rejected by policy, sent to an unresolvable model, or failed upstream. The log has no column for a prompt, completion, or upstream error text; the panel states that rather than showing an expandable row with nothing in it. One deployment wide default soft alert percentage for budget warnings. A project with its own alert threshold keeps using that value — changing the default here does not override it. Turning alerting off stops the warning only; the gateway still bills and still refuses a call that exceeds a budget. Retries, timeouts, fallback chains, key weighting, and semantic caching are not configurable from here or anywhere else in the product — the gateway runs its defaults for all of them.

title: Admin console overview
text: The admin console is a separate application at /admin/app , distinct from the main Elitea app. It is where an administrator manages the deployment as a whole: users, projects, authentication, the LLM proxy, budgets, branding, and platform wide configuration. Open the admin console Sign in to Elitea normally, then navigate to /admin/app . The console renders only if your account holds at least one administration mode permission — otherwise you see an access denied screen instead of an empty shell. Every individual page still enforces its own permission on the server on every request; the console's own check only decides whether it is worth rendering the navigation at all. Navigation groups The sidebar has two groups. Delete, promote, suspend, and review activity for any account. The permission matrix, across the central, public, and support scopes. Suspend, create, delete, and manage membership for every project. The global secret vault, merged into every project. Application access requests waiting on a decision. Authentication, LLM Proxy, MCP servers, banner, maintenance, e mail, and more, as a set of schema driven sections. The white label pack — colors, assets, and fonts. The outbound mail relay. Feature toggles: MCP exposure, publishing, analytics, Help Center, Support Assistant, Voice. A read only provider registry; most of it reports "not available" rather than data. Which toolkit types this deployment offers, and to which projects. Budgets, rate limits, allowlists, credential policy, and routing rules the LLM gateway enforces. Per project and per member spend limits. The deployment wide record of what happened. Cron schedules and background job status. There is no LiteLLM section. LiteLLM has been replaced by a standalone gateway service; its former admin screen is gone rather than kept as a dead link. A "Service Descriptors" entry is present even though the legacy admin UI never linked to it — it now answers honestly that this platform has no external provider hub, which is more useful than a page nothing could reach. What each page can and cannot decide window injected permission flags in the console are presentation only: they decide what the sidebar shows, never what a request is allowed to do. Every read and write is re authorized on the server against the actual permission that route requires. A typed URL to a page your account cannot use still reaches it — and still gets refused there.

title: Projects
text: The admin Projects page is the deployment wide project list. Every project — team or personal — appears here, regardless of who owns it. This is the one place an administrator sees and acts on every project at once, rather than one project's own Settings page at a time. Manage an existing project Search the table by name. A suspended project's members lose access until it is unsuspended. Both are available from the project's row menu. Export to CSV downloads the current list. Create or delete a project Both actions run a multi step process rather than a single database write: creating a project provisions its record, quota, dedicated schema, permission set, a system user and token, vault secrets, storage buckets, and vector store together; deleting one reverses the same steps, ending in dropping the project's schema. Each step's status is tracked individually, and a failed attempt is compensated rather than left half applied. Deleting a project destroys its data irreversibly. There is no undo. There is no self service request flow Every project is created by an administrator from this page. There is no in app way for a member to request a new project and have it approved — unlike application access, which does have a request/approval flow (see App requests and toolkit types). Not available yet: a self service "request a project" flow mirroring the App Requests moderation pattern (tracked in 871). Until then, ask your administrator directly to create a project for your team.

title: Schedules and tasks
text: Two admin pages cover recurring and running work: Schedules & Tasks for cron schedules, and Tasks for a live view of background jobs. Manage schedules Open Schedules & Tasks . Its Schedules tab lists cron bound platform jobs (for example, indexing schedules) with a live read and write — the scheduler service polls this table every minute and dispatches whatever is due. Each row pairs a cron expression with the platform operation it runs. Disabling a row stops it from being dispatched without deleting it. Open a schedule's history drawer for its past occurrences. The page's own "Tasks" tab is a permanent notice, not a table: it describes maintenance operations from the legacy plugin runtime, which this platform does not have and has no plan to add. It answers as unavailable rather than as an empty list, so "nothing is running" and "this deployment cannot see what is running" are never shown identically. See what is running Open the separate Tasks page for a live view of background work this platform actually tracks: index runs, agent turns, toolkit tool calls, scheduled occurrences, and evaluation runs. Narrow the list to one kind of task. The cancel control only appears on rows the server reports as cancellable — a task past that point does not offer it, rather than offering a control that would mostly answer with a conflict. There is no start control and no log tail here. Starting a task and reading its output are not modeled by this page — a task's output is its own artifact rather than a live log stream.

title: Secrets
text: Admin Secrets is a different store from a project's own Settings › Secrets page. A project's vault serves only that project; the global vault edited here is merged into {{secret.…}} resolution for every project on the deployment. Use the global vault for a value every project should be able to reference — a shared API key for an internal tool, a company wide webhook target — instead of copying the same secret into each project's own vault, where it would need to be kept in sync by hand. Manage a global secret The table lists every global secret by key; values are masked. Give it a key and a value. Reference it from any project as {{secret. }} , the same placeholder syntax used for a project scoped secret. A write here is platform wide — it changes what every project resolves for that key. There is no "hide" control for a global secret. A masked value already hides the secret; a separate hide action exists on neither this page nor its server route. The Internal tab is read only for every administrator, including super admins. It groups entries the platform wrote for itself rather than ones an operator authored — recognized by name ( auth token , project llm key , and bare 32 character hex reference names minted for configuration credential fields), not by a separate server flag. Those rows are shown rather than hidden so the vault's contents are fully accounted for, but nothing here offers to edit a value with no way of knowing what it is for.

title: Users and roles
text: Users and Roles are two related admin pages: Users acts on individual accounts, and Roles defines what each role is allowed to do. Manage users Open Users in the admin console. The table lists every account on the deployment, with search. Search by name or e mail. From the row menu: delete the account, grant or revoke the global admin role, or suspend/unsuspend it. A suspended account cannot sign in. Open the activity drawer for a per user view built on the same audit data as the Audit Trail page. Export to CSV downloads the current list. Invitations do not have a dedicated accept invite page. A new member accepts an invite by signing in; the invite is resolved by matching their identity on first login. Edit roles and permissions Open Roles . It shows a permission matrix across three scopes, each a tab: Central — the administration mode roles used across the deployment (the ones this admin console itself is gated on). Public Project — roles available inside the shared public project. Support Project — roles for the support project, if one is configured for this deployment. If none is configured, this tab reports that rather than an empty grid. Click a cell to grant or revoke that permission for that role, within the selected scope. Use the controls above the matrix. A new standard role only reaches projects that already exist once you use Apply to Projects next to it — creating the role does not retroactively push it everywhere by itself. The super admin column is disabled for anyone who is not a super admin, in the console only — this is a display convenience, not an enforced rule. The server does not treat super admin specially beyond the permission checks that apply to any other role.

title: Chat quick start
text: Chat is the center of Elitea: every agent, pipeline and toolkit is something you can bring into a conversation and talk to directly. Sign in and click Chat in the left sidebar (you're redirected there automatically if it's your first visit and you have no existing conversations). You'll see three areas: a conversation list on the left, the message history and composer in the center, and a participants panel on the right. Open the model selector at the bottom of the composer, choose a model, then type a message and press Enter or click send. A reply from the model confirms everything is wired correctly. Toolkits give the model access to external services such as Jira, GitHub or Confluence. Toolkits are created on their own page first, then attached to a conversation: 1. Go to Connect a toolkit quick start and create a Jira toolkit (or use one you already have), including its credential. 2. Back in chat, click the + button above the composer and open Toolkits . 3. Select your toolkit from the list. It appears in the participants panel and the model can now call its tools. 4. Ask something the toolkit can answer, for example "Find all open bugs in project ABC". The + menu only lists toolkits, agents, pipelines and MCP connections that already exist — there's no "create new" option inside chat itself. Create the entity on its own page first, then attach it here. Click the paperclip icon in the composer, or drag a file into the message area, to give the model something to analyze. See Attach files to a conversation for supported types and size limits. Reuse a conversation as an agent Once a conversation is configured the way you like — model, toolkits, instructions — you can save that setup as an agent so you don't have to rebuild it every time: 1. Create the agent on its own page at /agents/create , with the same toolkits and instructions you used in chat. 2. Back in chat, open the + menu, go to Agents , and select it as a participant. 3. From then on, selecting that agent brings its whole configuration into the conversation. You can also edit an agent's instructions from inside a conversation once it's already a participant — see Edit agents, pipelines, toolkits and MCPs from chat. Try a public agent Other users in your project may have published agents you can reuse without building your own: 1. Open the + menu, go to Agents , and look for items marked Public . 2. Select one to add it as a participant. 3. Send a message — the agent responds using its own instructions and toolkits. You can also browse public agents directly at /elitea catalog or under a user's public profile. See Use public items from chat for the full picture.

title: Configure an AI provider
text: Before anyone can chat or run an agent, a project needs at least one configured AI provider. Elitea supports seven provider kinds, and you configure each one the same way: pick a type, fill in its connection details, save. Go to Settings → AI Providers ( /settings/model configuration ). Configurations are grouped by kind: LLM, embedding, vector store, image generation, speech to text and text to speech. Click Create and choose a type, or go directly to /settings/create configuration/ (for example open ai , azure open ai , ai dial , anthropic , ollama , amazon bedrock , vertex ai , or vllm ). Fields vary by provider — see the table below. Give the configuration a display name for identification, then save. Once the provider connection exists, add the specific model it serves (display name, the exact model identifier the provider expects, context window, max output tokens). The model then appears in the model selector across chat, agents and pipelines. The most recently added model becomes the default for new conversations. Provider fields | Field | Notes | | | | | API key | Required for OpenAI and Anthropic; optional for Ollama and vLLM, which are commonly self hosted with no key | | Endpoint ( api base ) | Defaults to the provider's public API; override it for a self hosted or proxied endpoint | | Field | Notes | | | | | API key | Required | | Endpoint ( api base ) | Your Azure resource URL, or your DIAL host | | API version | Optional for DIAL, required for Azure (for example 2024 02 01 ) | | Field | Notes | | | | | AWS access key ID | Required | | AWS secret access key | Required | | AWS region | Required, for example us east 1 | | Field | Notes | | | | | Google Cloud project | Required | | Location | Required, for example us central1 | | Service account JSON | Required — paste the whole service account credentials document | The field names above are the LLM gateway's own credential keys, not display labels this form invents — they're what actually gets sent through when a model call is made, which matters if you're troubleshooting a configuration that saves but doesn't resolve. Never paste a real API key or service account document into a screenshot or shared document. Treat every field above marked as a key or secret the same way you'd treat a password. An administrator can also configure providers globally, shared across every project, from the admin console's LLM Proxy section — useful for a team wide default model that individual projects don't need to configure themselves.

title: Connect a toolkit quick start
text: Toolkits give a model access to an external service — searching Jira issues, reading a GitHub repository, browsing a Confluence space, and more. You create a toolkit once, then attach it to any conversation, agent or pipeline as a participant. Go to /toolkits/create . Tiles are grouped by category (code repositories, project management, documentation, testing, and so on); pick the service you want to connect. Most toolkit types need a saved credential. In the toolkit form, open the credential dropdown and either select an existing one or create a new one — this opens Create a credential, where you fill in the service's base URL and authentication (an API token, a username and password, or an app key, depending on the type). Save the credential, then refresh the dropdown in the toolkit form to pick it up. Give the toolkit a name, fill in any service specific fields (repository, project key, space, bucket name, and so on), and choose which tools to enable — each toolkit type ships a fixed list of tools (for example Jira's "Search using JQL" and "Create issue"). If the type supports indexing, you'll also pick an embedding model and a vector store here; see Indexing overview. Click Create . The toolkit now appears in your toolkit list at /toolkits/all . To use it, open a conversation, click the + button, go to Toolkits , and select it — the model can now call its tools. A few common toolkit types | Type | Credential fields | Typical use | | | | | | Jira | Base URL, and either username + API key or a bearer token | Search and create issues with JQL | | Confluence | Base URL, and either username + API key or a bearer token | Search and read documentation pages | | GitHub | Access token, username + password, or a GitHub App key (or none, for public repositories) | Read files, list pull requests, create issues | | Figma | Personal access token | Read file structure, images and comments | | TestRail | Instance URL, e mail, password or API key | Read and create test cases | | Artifact | A bucket name (lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens) | Store and retrieve files agents or chat attachments read and write | Some toolkit types are not available on every deployment: which ones appear depends on the agent worker your deployment runs (Rust or Python), and an administrator can additionally restrict types per project on the Toolkit types admin page. If a type you expect is missing from the tile grid, check with your administrator before assuming the connection is broken. See Use credentials for the project vs private credential distinction, and Create a secret if you'd rather reference a value from the project vault than paste it into a credential field.

title: Create an artifact bucket
text: Artifacts are files stored in project scoped buckets — a place for chat attachments, agent generated files, and anything else a workflow needs to persist between turns. Artifacts must be enabled for your deployment (the ELITEA ARTIFACTS ENABLED capability flag). If the Artifacts menu item is missing, ask your administrator. Go to /artifacts . Click Create bucket ( /artifacts/create bucket ) and give it a unique name (lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens). Set a retention period in days — files older than that are automatically deleted — or leave it unset to keep files indefinitely. Open the bucket and upload a file, or drag one in. You can download, pin, or delete files and buckets from the same view. Edit an existing bucket Open /artifacts and select a bucket, or go directly to /artifacts/create bucket?bucket= , to change its retention window or delete it. Deleting a bucket removes every file inside it — there's no separate "empty the bucket" step, so confirm you no longer need its contents first. Let an agent use a bucket An agent or a pipeline reaches a bucket through an Artifact toolkit: create one at /toolkits/create with type Artifact, pointing at your bucket name, and enable the file tools you want the agent to call (create, read, list, append, delete). See Connect a toolkit quick start. Chat attachments also land in a bucket automatically, without you creating one yourself — see Attach files to a conversation. Toolkit types that support indexing can also index straight into artifact storage, which is what lets an agent search over a bucket's contents instead of only reading files back one at a time. Related Manage artifact buckets and files Index data from a source

title: Create a credential
text: A credential holds the authentication details a toolkit needs to reach an external service — a base URL, a token, or a username and password. You create one, then attach it to any toolkit of the matching type. Go to /credentials/all and click Create , or go directly to /credentials/create credential/ for a specific service. Select the credential type (GitHub, Jira, Azure DevOps, and so on). Fields vary by type — most ask for a base URL plus a token, or a username and password. Where a field expects a secret, create it first at Create a secret so it's available in the dropdown. Project credentials are shared with everyone on the project; private credentials are visible only to you. Pick whichever matches who should be able to use it. Give the credential a clear name and save. It's now available in any toolkit form that takes this credential type. Attach it to a toolkit 1. Open /toolkits/create/ (or edit an existing toolkit of the matching type). 2. Open the credential dropdown and select the credential you created — or create a new one on the fly from the same dropdown, as a project or private credential. 3. Save the toolkit. It now authenticates using this credential. If your credential doesn't appear in a toolkit's dropdown, confirm it saved successfully and that you're working in the same project — private credentials only appear to the user who created them. Good practice Use descriptive names for both credentials and toolkits. Reference secrets from the vault instead of pasting raw values into credential fields — see Create a secret. Rotate credentials and secrets periodically, and remove ones you no longer use.

title: Create a personal access token
text: A personal access token authenticates you (or a script, or an IDE plugin) to Elitea's API without a browser session. Go to Settings → Personal tokens ( /settings/tokens ). Use the project switcher at the top if you need a token scoped to a different project. Click the + icon, give the token a descriptive name, and set an expiration date. Click Generate . Copy the token immediately. The token value is shown only once, in the dialog right after you generate it. If you close the dialog without copying it, you cannot retrieve the value again — delete the token and generate a new one instead. Use the token Send it as a bearer token against Elitea's API (see API usage). From the token list, you can also pick a model and download a ready made settings file (VS Code JSON or JetBrains XML) pre filled with your token, the model and your project id. This session could not confirm which current IDE extension or plugin reads that generated settings file — the legacy documentation pointed to an "Elitea Code" VS Code/JetBrains extension that has no trace in the current codebase or its integrations. The settings download feature itself is real and working; what consumes the file downstream could not be verified. (tracked) Good practice Keep tokens confidential — never commit one to version control. Name tokens by what uses them, so you know what breaks if you revoke one. Set an expiration date and rotate tokens regularly. Delete tokens you no longer use. If you work across multiple projects, create a separate token per project.

title: Create a secret
text: The Secrets vault stores sensitive values — passwords, tokens, API keys — encrypted, so credentials and toolkits can reference them by name instead of carrying a raw value. Go to Settings → Secrets ( /settings/secrets ). Click the + icon, give it a descriptive name, and paste the value. Once saved, the secret appears in the secrets table. Click the eye icon to reveal its value, click the hidden value to copy it, and use the row actions to edit or delete it. Reference a secret from a credential Instead of pasting a raw token or password into a credential field, reference the secret you stored: 1. Open or create a credential ( /credentials/create credential ). 2. On a field like API key, token or password, switch it to reference a secret instead of typing a value. 3. Pick your secret from the dropdown. The field now stores {{secret. }} rather than the raw value, and the credential resolves it at call time. If you rotate the secret's value later, every credential referencing it picks up the new value automatically — you don't have to update each credential individually. This is the project level vault, scoped to one project. There's also a separate global vault an administrator manages from the admin console, whose secrets are merged into every project's {{secret.…}} references. If a secret name looks unfamiliar, check both. Good practice Never hardcode credentials — store sensitive values as secrets and reference them. Use one secret per integration rather than reusing a single value everywhere. Rotate secrets regularly, and delete ones you no longer use. Name secrets so their purpose is obvious to a teammate later (for example jira service account token rather than token1 ) — the name is the only hint anyone gets before revealing the value. Related Create a credential Settings › Secrets

title: Install Elitea
text: Elitea ships two deployment paths: a one host Compose stack for evaluation and small teams, and a Helm chart for Kubernetes. Neither path bundles PostgreSQL, Redis, NATS, object storage or an ingress controller — you bring your own. Choose a deployment path The standalone stack ( docker compose.standalone full.yml ) runs the whole topology — elitea web, elitea main, the LLM gateway, the agent worker, and supporting services — on one machine, driven by deploy/scripts/standalone stack.sh : A fresh up bootstraps the schema, the vector extension, the artifact bucket, RBAC roles, and the worker's runtime authorization automatically. You do not need to run any of the seed subcommands — those exist only for local development and end to end testing. The one setting you still set by hand is GATEWAY EGRESS ALLOWLIST on the LLM gateway service: a comma separated host:port list the gateway checks a saved credential's base URL against before it will proxy to it. It defaults to the compose network's own model services. Add your own model host to it before saving a credential that points there, or the gateway refuses the connection in a way that looks like the model is down. The Helm chart lives at deploy/helm/elitea/ , published as a signed OCI chart. Composition is app of apps: an ArgoCD Application in deploy/argocd/applications/ renders it, there is no separate umbrella chart. Two values must be supplied by you — the chart refuses to render while either is empty: llmGateway.env.GATEWAY SELF LLM ORIGINS — the origin the gateway advertises to itself. llmGateway.egressPosture — the gateway's default egress policy. You also point the chart at Kubernetes Secrets you create out of band, rather than putting anything secret in a values file: postgresql.existingSecret / postgresql.key — the database connection string. runtime.material.secretName — the runtime's signing keys, certificates and Redis credentials (only if you enable the runtime plane, below). fileConfig.authConfig.material.secretName — the authentication plane's Redis credentials and signing keys. Pick a values file to start from: values.yaml (base, minimal capabilities), values standalone.yaml (the full capability set, sized for roughly 200 PostgreSQL connections across up to four replicas), values auth minimal.yaml (the cheapest install that can still seed an AI provider through the UI), or values staging.yaml . Capability flags A handful of environment variables on elitea main turn whole capabilities on or off; each one gates a route group at startup. The values files above set sensible combinations, but if you are assembling your own: | Flag | What it gates | | | | | ELITEA ARTIFACTS ENABLED | The Artifacts (bucket/file storage) menu and API | | ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS ENABLED | The AI Providers configuration plane (requires authentication and a project id) | | ELITEA PROJECT INFO ENABLED | Project metadata endpoints | | ELITEA CONFIGURATIONS MUTATION ENABLED | Editing AI provider configurations (requires the configuration plane and the runtime plane) | | ELITEA INDEX TYPES ENABLED | Toolkit indexing | | ELITEA APPLICATION SKILLS ENABLED | Skills | | ELITEA RUNTIME ENABLED | Agent execution — the chat send path itself | | ELITEA INVENTORY SOURCE TYPES | Which source types Inventory can ingest (defaults to GitHub and Azure DevOps Repos) | ELITEA RUNTIME ENABLED is the one that matters most: without it, agents cannot run at all. Turning it on is a provisioning exercise, not a flag flip — it needs a signing keyring, mutually authenticated listeners and a workload session row, all of which the values files above provision for you. First login and setup The first account to sign in with a matching entry becomes a global administrator. Set the entry through your authentication configuration document, or through the environment variable ELITEA INITIAL GLOBAL ADMINS (a comma separated list) if your deployment has no such document — this is the usual path for a single sign on only install. Each entry takes one of three shapes: | Shape | Matches | | | | | oidc: | The OIDC subject claim, exactly as your identity provider issues it | | saml: | The SAML NameID | | email: | A verified e mail address (the login's identity token must assert email verified: true ) | The variable is empty by default, so a fresh install stays unprivileged until you opt in. The grant applies once: if the account already holds an administration role you leave it as is, and an account with none receives the grant on its next sign in. Open the deployment in your browser and sign in through your identity provider (or the Form plane, if configured). If your reference matches an ELITEA INITIAL GLOBAL ADMINS entry, you land with a global administrator role. Open the admin console at /admin/app/projects and create a project. Project creation is administrator only — Elitea has no self service "request a project" flow; every project starts with an administrator creating it and assigning members afterward. In your project, open Settings → AI Providers ( /settings/create configuration/open ai for OpenAI, or pick another provider type) and save a model configuration. See Configure an AI provider for the full field list per provider. Everything from here on — chat, agents, toolkits — is configured entirely from the UI; no direct database access is required. After install | Path | What's there | | | | | /docs/ | This documentation site | | /api/docs | The OpenAPI reference UI | | /admin/app | The admin console | | /app/{projectId}/mcp/… | Elitea's own MCP server, for external MCP clients | | /api/v2/scim/v2 | SCIM provisioning, if you connect an identity provider that supports it | Observability runs over OpenTelemetry through elitea main's collector proxy — there is no Langfuse or other third party APM integration.

title: Glossary
text: This glossary defines terms used throughout the platform. Where the current UI uses a different name than older documentation, the current name is listed first. A Agent — A configurable virtual assistant that combines instructions, an AI model, and optional toolkits to perform tasks and answer questions. AI Providers — The Settings section where you configure LLM, embedding, vector storage, image generation, speech recognition, and text to speech models and their credentials for a project. Artifact — A file stored in a project bucket, shared between agents, pipelines, and conversations for temporary storage and context. B Bucket — A container in Artifacts that groups related files under a single retention policy. C Canvas — The in chat editor for code, table, and Mermaid diagram blocks generated during a conversation. It edits the block created in the current turn; it does not open or save previously stored files. Catalog (Elitea Catalog) — The shared library of published agents and skills, browsable and searchable across all your projects. Older documentation calls this "Agent HUB" or "Agents Studio." Chat — The conversational interface where you interact with models, agents, pipelines, toolkits, MCP servers, and teammates. Context management — Automated pruning and summarization of older conversation messages so long conversations stay within a model's token limit. Configured in Settings › Memory. Conversation Starter — A predefined prompt configured on an agent or pipeline that helps users begin an interaction. Credential — Securely stored authentication information (API key, token, or similar) used by a toolkit or AI provider to connect to an external service. E Entity — General term for the main things you create and manage: agents, pipelines, skills, toolkits, and artifacts. I Indexing — The process of extracting content from files and toolkits and storing it in a vector database so it can be retrieved with semantic search. L LLM (Large Language Model) — The AI model that processes and generates text for a conversation, agent, or pipeline. M MCP (Model Context Protocol) — A protocol that lets Elitea connect to external MCP servers over HTTP, exposing their tools to agents, pipelines, and conversations. Elitea itself also acts as an MCP server, exposing agents (tagged mcp ) and MCP enabled toolkit tools to external MCP clients. Memory — In Settings, the personal page that configures context window management (pruning, summarization) for new conversations. Persistent, cross conversation long term memory is not available yet. N Node — A single step in a pipeline (agent, toolkit, MCP, LLM, decision, router, state modifier, printer, or human in the loop) that the pipeline compiler can run. P Participant — Anything active in a conversation: a model, an agent, a pipeline, a toolkit, an MCP server, or a human teammate. Personal Access Token (PAT) — A token you generate in Settings › Personal Tokens for programmatic API access or IDE integration. Pipeline — A visual, multi step workflow connecting agents, toolkits, and control flow nodes into a repeatable automated process. Project Context — A project level background document that Elitea applies to every AI interaction in the project, giving agents shared domain terminology, workflows, and constraints. Public Project — A shared, deployment wide project (separate from your personal and team projects) that some settings sections — Project Context, Prompts, Environment — are scoped to. R Remote MCP — An MCP connection to an HTTP/HTTPS based server, configured like any other toolkit type. S Skill — A reusable, Markdown based instruction set attached to an agent version and invoked on demand with ~skill name . Support Assistant — An AI powered help widget, embedded in the platform, that is aware of the project and page you are on. T Tag — A label used to categorize and filter agents, pipelines, and other entities. Toolkit — A configured integration — with an external service or an Elitea native capability — that gives agents and pipelines the ability to act. See the toolkit catalogue. Token — A unit of text used by AI models to measure input and output size, and also the name for a personal access token depending on context. V Version — A saved snapshot of an agent, pipeline, or skill. Agents and pipelines support multiple named versions; skills currently support only one implicit base version. Vector Storage — The storage layer (PGVector) used for embeddings and semantic retrieval, configured per project in AI Providers. W Webhook — A callback based mechanism some pipeline triggers use to start a run from an external event. Webhook management is available through the API only; there is no management page in the UI yet. Terms you may see in older material These names appear in earlier documentation but describe something that has changed shape or is no longer part of the platform. They are listed here so the term is not a dead end. The shared library of published agents and skills is now the Catalog tab, reachable from the sidebar. Elitea's MCP server is streamable HTTP only. There is no local STDIO MCP client or server; only Remote MCP connections exist. No trace of dedicated VS Code or IntelliJ extensions exists in the current platform. Personal tokens still expose IDE settings snippets on the Personal Tokens page. Tracing is provided through OpenTelemetry via the platform's own collector; there is no Langfuse integration. These were older application types. The current agent type values are openai (default), react , dial , and pipeline . Not exposed in the current model settings UI. Use Temperature or Creativity/Reasoning instead, depending on the model. "Collection" as a distinct entity type is not present in the current platform; content is organized with tags and folders instead.

title: Overview of the Elitea platform
text: Elitea is a platform for creating and running AI agents and automated workflows, and for chatting with AI models directly. It combines several building blocks that you configure once and reuse across your project. Key building blocks Agents : virtual assistants that combine instructions, an AI model, and optional toolkits to perform tasks — from answering questions to creating tickets in Jira. Pipelines : visual workflows that chain agents, toolkits, and logic nodes into a multi step, repeatable process. Chat : the conversational interface where you talk to models, agents, pipelines, toolkits, and MCP servers, and where you build and edit them inline. Skills : reusable, named instruction sets you attach to agents so several agents can share the same behavior. Toolkits : integrations with external services (Jira, GitHub, Confluence, and more) that give agents and pipelines the ability to act outside the chat. Credentials : securely stored authentication details (API keys, tokens) that toolkits and AI providers use to connect. Artifacts : bucket based file storage shared between agents, pipelines, and conversations. Indexing : turns documents and connected sources into searchable vector indexes so agents can retrieve grounded context instead of relying on conversation history alone. MCP servers : remote Model Context Protocol servers that add external tools to your agents, pipelines, and conversations. Applications : purpose built integrations — DeepWiki and Inventory — that turn a code repository into browsable documentation or a queryable component graph. See DeepWiki and Inventory. Elitea Catalog : a shared library of published agents and skills you can browse, fork, and start using immediately. Accessing Elitea 1. Open the deployment URL in a modern browser. 2. If you are not signed in, you are redirected to your organization's sign in screen (OIDC, SAML, or a Form based login, depending on how your administrator configured authentication). 3. After signing in you land in Chat . 4. Use the Project Selector at the top of the sidebar to switch between your personal project and any team projects you belong to. 5. Select the Elitea icon at the top of the sidebar to open the full menu list — Chat, Agents, Pipelines, Skills, Toolkits, Applications, Credentials, Artifacts, Catalog, and Settings. There is no separate login or password reset page inside Elitea itself — sign in is handled by your identity provider or by the platform's Form based login, and invited users accept an invite by signing in for the first time. Ready to see what's possible? Continue with key concepts, or jump straight into the chat quick start. For definitions of terms used throughout the platform, see the Glossary.

title: Key concepts
text: Elitea is built from a small set of concepts that combine to form larger workflows. Each one has its own menu; this page gives you the mental model before you dive in. Agent An agent is a virtual assistant you configure with instructions, an AI model, and optional toolkits. It interprets a task, decides which tools to call, and acts — from searching the web to creating a Jira ticket — without you scripting every step. A useful agent combines: clear instructions describing its job, one or more toolkits for the services it needs to reach, and a model suited to the task's complexity. See Agents. Skill A skill is a reusable, Markdown based instruction set you attach to an agent. Where an agent is a whole assistant, a skill is a focused capability — a checklist, a persona, a domain procedure — that multiple agents can share. Update the skill once and every agent that has it attached picks up the change; invoke it mid conversation with ~skill name . See Skills. Pipeline A pipeline is a visual, multi step workflow that connects agents, toolkits, and control flow nodes (decisions, routers, state updates) into a repeatable process. Use a pipeline when a task needs more than one stage — for example, reading a requirement, drafting a user story, then generating a test case — with each stage's output feeding the next. See Pipelines. Credential A credential securely stores the authentication details — API keys, tokens, or other secrets — that a toolkit or AI provider needs to connect to an external service. Credentials are created once and can be reused across multiple toolkits and agents, and can be scoped to a project or kept private to you. See Credentials. Toolkit A toolkit is a configured integration with an external service (Jira, GitHub, Confluence, and dozens more) or an Elitea native capability (Artifact storage, a custom OpenAPI connection). Once configured with a credential and a set of enabled tools, a toolkit can be attached to any agent, pipeline, or conversation in the project. See Toolkits and the toolkit catalogue. Conversation A conversation is an interactive chat session where you talk to models, agents, pipelines, toolkits, MCP servers, and — in team projects — human teammates, all as participants in the same thread. Conversations keep their own history and can be organized into folders, shared, or replayed. See Chat. Artifact An artifact is a file stored in a bucket that agents, pipelines, and conversations can read from and write to as shared, temporary storage. Buckets have a retention policy and are organized per project, so generated files (reports, exported data, chat attachments) have somewhere durable to live between turns. See Artifacts. For definitions of additional terms, see the Glossary.

title: Onboarding tips
text: The first time you sign in, Elitea takes you to the onboarding screen before dropping you into Chat. Use it, and this page, to get oriented quickly. Find your way around The Elitea icon at the top of the sidebar opens the full menu: Chat, Agents, Pipelines, Skills, Toolkits, Applications, Credentials, Artifacts, and Settings. The Project Selector at the top of the sidebar switches between your personal project and any team projects you belong to. Start experimenting in your personal project before sharing work with a team. The socket connection indicator on the Elitea logo shows whether your browser has a live connection to the server (green) or has lost it (red). A ? button near the bottom of the sidebar opens the Help Center with documentation, release notes, and tutorials configured by your administrator. Your first hour Chat is where everything comes together. Start a new conversation and send a message directly to a model — no setup required for a plain conversation. See Chat. In the Participants panel, add a toolkit (for example GitHub or Jira) so the conversation can act on an external service. Create the toolkit and its credential right from the chat editor. See Toolkits and Credentials. Add an Agent participant and use its inline editor to write instructions, pick a model, and attach the toolkit you just created. See Agents. Mention the agent with in the chat input, activate it, and send a message. Iterate on the instructions until the responses look right. Once a task needs more than one agent or a decision point, move it into a pipeline. Keep learning Chat quick start for a guided first conversation. Connect toolkits quick start for a full toolkit walkthrough. Key concepts for what each building block does. Glossary for definitions of terms used throughout the platform. Interactive, in product tours may also be available from the Help Center, depending on what your administrator has configured.

title: Build an agent with AI
text: Build with AI turns a short, natural language description into a starting agent draft — name, description, instructions, welcome message and conversation starters. Nothing is created until you review the draft and confirm. Generate a draft Go to Agents , click Create , and open the General section of the new agent form. Click Build with AI (sparkle icon) in the section header. The button only appears if you have permission to create or update agents in the project, and the project has a default LLM model configured. Enter what the agent is for, what tasks it should handle, and any tone or constraints you want. Press Enter to generate (Shift+Enter adds a line break instead). Elitea returns a draft with Name (up to 32 characters), Description , Instructions , Welcome message (up to 768 characters) and up to four Conversation starters . Every field is editable before you create the agent. Use Back to prompt to revise your description and regenerate. Click Create Agent . The agent is created with the reviewed fields and the project's default model, and the page opens on its Configuration tab for further setup. Not available yet: AI suggested toolkits, agents, pipelines, MCPs or skills to attach to the new agent — the draft only generates the text fields above; the review form shows no resource suggestions. (tracked in 881) The same generator is available for a skill ( /skills/create ) and for project context (Settings › public project context) — the underlying draft endpoint serves all three, so the same "describe it, review it, create it" flow applies there too. See Create and share a skill. Edit instructions with AI Once an agent exists, its Configuration tab's General section can show an Edit with AI button next to the Instructions field. It needs a model configured on the agent's version and an AI configuration the deployment has enabled; if either is missing, the button does not appear at all rather than failing on click. Click Edit with AI . Enter what you want changed about the instructions — for example, tightening scope or changing tone. Elitea proposes replacement instructions and shows a highlighted diff against the current text. Applying the suggestion fills in the Instructions field, the same way any manual edit would. Save the agent version afterward to keep the change. This tool edits instructions only — it does not touch the name, welcome message, conversation starters, or attached toolkits/skills, and it has no separate "save as version" step of its own; use the agent's normal version controls for that (see Version agents and pipelines). Creating or editing an agent from inside a chat conversation's "+" menu is not available — that menu only attaches existing agents as participants. Use /agents/create for a new agent, or the standalone agent editor above. See Edit agents, pipelines, toolkits and MCPs from chat. Guides and references Agents overview — creating and configuring agents manually Publish agents and skills Version agents and pipelines Toolkits overview

title: Version agents and pipelines
text: Agents and pipelines keep a version history. The first save always creates a version named base ; from there you can keep editing base, or branch off into named versions you can compare, publish, and share independently. Save a version Every new agent or pipeline starts on the base version. Edit and save it as many times as you like — nothing else is required to keep working. When you want to preserve the current configuration, click Save As Version in the toolbar and enter a name: alphanumeric characters, hyphens and underscores only, no spaces, up to 20 characters, and unique within the entity. base is reserved and cannot be reused as a custom name. Use the version dropdown next to the entity name to switch versions. Saving always updates whichever version is currently selected — switch first, then save, if you want to update a specific version rather than base. Set a default version A default version is the one automatically selected when the agent is added to a conversation, used as a toolkit in another agent or pipeline, or exposed as an MCP toolkit. Pin a version as default from the version dropdown or the toolbar's three dot menu, then confirm in the dialog. Only Draft versions can be set as default; published versions and the currently set default cannot be deleted until you designate a different one. If no version is explicitly set as default, base is used implicitly. Compare versions When an entity has two or more versions, a Compare versions action becomes available from the toolbar's three dot menu. It opens a read only, side by side comparison of any two versions — useful for checking what changed before you set a new default or publish. Share a version Copy link copies a direct URL to the currently selected version to your clipboard. Anyone with access to the project can open it; the link does not grant access by itself, and it stops resolving if the version is later deleted. Export downloads the current version as a Markdown file. If the version references nested agents or pipelines, the export becomes a ZIP containing one Markdown file per entity (the main one plus each dependency). Import the file into another project with Import and export entities. Publishing an agent (see Publish agents and skills) only exports its published versions. Delete a version You can delete any version except base and the current default. If other agents or pipelines reference the version you're deleting, a replacement version dialog lists them and lets you pick which version they should point to instead; the system updates those references automatically. Not available yet: skill version history, compare, or rollback — a skill has a single implicit version and none of the controls on this page apply to it. (tracked in 874) Guides and references Agents overview Pipelines overview Import and export entities

title: Fork an agent or toolkit
text: Forking copies an agent, pipeline or toolkit into a different project in place — no file download or upload, unlike export/import. When to fork instead of exporting Use fork when you're moving an entity between projects you already have access to — for example, taking a working agent from a private project into a shared team project, or copying a public agent from the catalogue into your own project so you can customize it. Use import and export instead when the destination is a different deployment entirely, or when you want a file you can archive, review, or send to someone outside the platform. Open the agent or pipeline and select the version you want to copy — only the currently selected version is forked. Click the toolbar's three dot menu and choose Fork . In the dialog, pick the destination project. You need fork permission there. If the agent uses other agents as nested toolkits, those are forked alongside it into the same target project. Confirm. Elitea copies the entity into the target project and takes you to it there. The original model is kept if it's available in the destination project; otherwise the fork falls back to a model that is. Toolkit credentials are never copied — reconfigure them manually in the target project after forking. Toolkits can be forked the same way from their own three dot menu. Guides and references Import and export entities Agents overview Toolkits overview Forking creates an independent copy — the fork and the original aren't linked afterward, so a later change to either one doesn't affect the other.

title: Import and export entities
text: Export lets you back up or move an agent, pipeline, toolkit, skill or conversation as a file; import brings an exported agent or pipeline back into a project. Export an agent or pipeline Open the agent or pipeline, then use Export in the toolbar's three dot menu. The download is a JSON document containing the entity's currently selected version, its associated toolkits, and any skills attached to it. Authentication credentials are never included — you reconfigure them after import. Import an agent or pipeline On the Agents or Pipelines list, click Import and choose a .json export file. Elitea reads the file and shows the agent or pipeline names, and how many toolkits and skills it carries, before anything is created. Confirm the import. The entity is created in your current project using the file's exported configuration; model settings fall back to the project's own configured LLM, embedding and vector store defaults where the export didn't carry a credential. Any toolkit that needs a credential (API key, token) must be reconfigured manually — exports never carry secrets. Importing requires import permission in the destination project; the Import button is disabled without it. A file that isn't valid JSON, or has no exported agents in it, is rejected with an explanation rather than silently failing. Export and import a skill Skills export as a Markdown file ( Export on a skill's page) and import the same way, from the Skills list's Import button. See Create and share a skill for the full skill lifecycle. Export a toolkit A toolkit's three dot menu offers Export , producing a file with its type, name, settings and enabled tools — again with credentials excluded. Export a conversation A conversation can be exported from its options menu, producing a copy of the conversation for backup or sharing outside the app. Guides and references Agents overview Pipelines overview Version agents and pipelines Fork an agent or toolkit

title: Publish agents and skills
text: Publishing submits an agent version or a skill for review, then makes it available in the shared catalog (Agent HUB / the Elitea Catalog's Skills tab) once approved. Pipelines cannot be published — this applies to agents and skills only. Publish an agent version Open the agent, select the version you want to publish, and choose Publish from the toolbar's three dot menu. Enter a unique version name (letters, numbers, dots, hyphens, underscores; up to 50 characters) and pick a category from the project's configured list. Agree to the publishing terms to continue. Elitea runs an automated AI review of the version and reports critical issues, warnings, and suggestions. A failing result stops the wizard here; a pass or warning only result lets you continue. Confirm to submit. The version goes to the moderation queue for admin review before it appears in the catalog. Any skills attached to the agent are kept and still work at runtime, but publishing the agent does not separately publish those skills as their own catalog entries. The Publish action is hidden if your role lacks the publish permission. If it's visible but disabled with a policy tooltip, the platform has restricted publishing to an allowed list of projects — ask your administrator. Publish a skill Skills publish the same way, from a skill's three dot menu — but a skill has a single version, so there's no version selector: you publish the skill as it currently stands. On the skill's page, choose Publish . Enter a version name and pick a category, as with an agent. Elitea runs a set of structural checks (not an AI review) and reports which passed, which are warnings, and which block publishing. A failing check must be fixed before you can continue — there's no "publish anyway" past a failure. Confirm. The skill is submitted for moderation, same as an agent. Unpublish Unpublishing removes the item from the catalog immediately (no moderation step) and returns its status to Draft. You get an in app notification when your agent or skill is published, rejected, or unpublished by a moderator. Guides and references Publish moderation queue (admin) Elitea Catalog Version agents and pipelines

title: Add teammates to a conversation
text: Adding human teammates to a conversation only works in team projects, not in your personal project. Add a teammate In the Participants panel, click the add participants icon. A dialog opens with a search box listing project members. Search by name and select one or more people. Click Add . The people you selected appear in the Users section of the Participants panel and receive a notification that they've been added. Mention a teammate Type @ in the message box to open a suggestion list of everyone in the conversation, then pick a name (or select Everyone , shown once the conversation has two or more human participants, to notify the whole group). A mention only directs the message at that person — agents and pipelines in the conversation don't treat it as an instruction to act. Remove a teammate Open the Users list in the Participants panel, hover over the person's name, and click the delete icon that appears, then confirm. You can't remove yourself this way. Who can see the conversation Adding a teammate only shares the conversation with the people you explicitly add — it does not make the conversation visible to the rest of the project unless someone also marks it public (see Use chat for visibility rules). Removing a teammate stops their access going forward but doesn't retroactively hide messages they've already read. This is different from adding an agent, pipeline, or toolkit as a participant — those are attached from the composer's + menu, not this dialog, and they don't count toward "teammates." See Use chat for that flow. Related Use chat

title: Attach files to a conversation
text: Attaching a file gives the model something concrete to analyze — a screenshot, a spreadsheet, a log file — right inside a conversation. Attach a file Click the + button above the composer, then Attach files . Use any of three methods: click to browse and select, drag a file from your computer into the message area, or paste an image from your clipboard. Type a message describing what you want done with the file, then send. Limits The exact file type allowlist and the maximum file size or count per message are configured per deployment rather than fixed in the client — this page does not state specific numbers because they could not be verified against a single value in source. If a file is rejected, the composer's error message names the limit that applies on your deployment. Where attached files go Every file you attach uploads to a shared attachments bucket automatically — you don't configure a bucket yourself. You can browse, download or delete anything in it from the Artifacts menu; see Artifacts for bucket management and retention. By default a bucket's files expire after 30 days, but this can be changed per bucket. Turn attachments on for an agent Attaching files works in a plain conversation without any setup. If you want attachments available every time a specific agent is used, enable it on the agent itself: 1. Open the agent's edit page and go to its Configuration tab. 2. Find Allow attachments under Modules and turn it on. 3. Save. Attach files now appears in the + menu whenever this agent is a participant. Enabling this toggle requires Editor or Admin permission on the project — anyone with access to a conversation can still attach files without touching the agent's configuration.

title: Manage conversation context
text: Every conversation, agent run, and pipeline execution tracks how many tokens its history is using and manages that automatically once the limit gets close. This is enabled by default — there's nothing to turn on to start seeing it. The context budget widget The widget appears once you've sent a first message. It has three views: Collapsed : a status line — green under the limit, orange over it. Compact : adds current token usage as a percentage, the message count, and how many summaries have been generated, plus an edit button. Expanded : the full configuration, in three sections — token management, summarization, and user instructions — plus a toggle to turn context management off entirely for this conversation. Configure it Click the widget's edit control to open the full settings: Max context tokens and preserve recent messages control how much history is kept before older messages are pruned or summarized. Automatic summarization compresses older messages into a summary once usage nears the limit, guided by your own summarization instructions and a target summary length. The target must stay below the max token limit — the form won't let you save otherwise. User instructions let you keep system messages pinned, pick a default persona for plain model chat, and add custom behavior instructions. Your personal defaults for these settings live in Settings › Memory; a conversation, agent, or pipeline can override them for itself. Why this matters A model can only see as much conversation history as fits in its context window. Without pruning or summarization, a long running conversation eventually pushes early messages out entirely, and the model loses track of what was said. Automatic summarization trades some detail for a much longer effective memory — the summary stands in for the messages it replaces, so the model still has a sense of what happened even after the original text is gone. Related Use chat

title: Edit agents, pipelines, toolkits and MCPs from chat
text: Once an agent, pipeline, toolkit, or MCP connection (an MCP connection is a kind of toolkit) is a participant in your conversation, you can open its editor inline and adjust it without switching pages. This page covers editing an existing participant — creating a brand new one still happens on its own create page, outside chat. Edit an existing participant If it isn't already in the conversation, attach it from the composer's + menu or by typing . See Use chat. Click the participant in the Participants panel, then click its settings icon (or hover and click the edit icon that appears). The inline editor opens for that entity type. Edit it and save — the change applies to that entity going forward, the same as editing it from its own page. What you can change per entity type Agent : instructions, model and model settings, and attached toolkits. See Build an agent with AI for the underlying fields. Pipeline : the flow and its nodes. See Use the flow editor. Toolkit or MCP connection : configuration, credential, and which tools are enabled. See Use credentials. Creating a new one Not available yet: creating a new agent, pipeline, toolkit, or MCP connection directly from a chat participant menu — the menu only lists existing items to attach, with no "create new" option. Use the standalone create pages instead: Create an agent, Create a pipeline, Create a toolkit, or create an MCP connection from the same toolkits area. Once created, come back to chat and attach it as a participant. (tracked in 867) Related Use chat Use canvas

title: Elitea MCP Tools (internal tool)
text: Elitea MCP Tools is a Python worker only internal tool. On a deployment running the Rust worker (the Helm default), it is skipped silently — the agent still answers, just without this capability. Elitea MCP Tools connects an agent to Elitea's own MCP server from inside a conversation, so it can discover and call other agents and toolkit tools that have been explicitly exposed, without you pre wiring every dependency. What becomes callable Other agents , if they carry the mcp tag. Each one becomes a callable that takes a single task description and returns that agent's final response. Agents without the tag are never listed, published or not. Toolkit tools , for any toolkit with its MCP option turned on. Each enabled tool becomes an individual callable with the toolkit's native input and output shape. Enable it In a conversation, click + in the composer, open Modules , and toggle Elitea MCP Tools on. To make it the default for every new conversation with a given agent, open that agent's configuration, find the module in its tools list, and save. Add the mcp tag to any agent you want this module to be able to call. On a toolkit, turn on its MCP option and select which of its tools are exposed. This page describes calling existing agents and toolkit tools through the module. Whether the module can also create or update agents and pipelines directly could not be verified against the current source and is not documented here as present. Related Use chat Manage your MCP servers

title: Use canvas
