text: Canvas turns a code block, table, or Mermaid diagram from an assistant's reply into its own editor, so you can refine it without leaving the conversation. Open canvas Ask a model to generate something canvas supports — a script, a Markdown table, or a Mermaid diagram — then click the edit (pencil) icon that appears on that block. This opens the canvas editor for just that piece of content. Syntax highlighted editing with its own undo/redo history. Use Copy to copy the current content to your clipboard, or Save to persist your edits back to the conversation. A spreadsheet like view over the Markdown table. Edit cells directly, then Save , or export the table to CSV or XLSX. Edit the underlying Mermaid source with a live preview, then Save . Real time collaboration If more than one person has the same conversation open, everyone sees who else is editing a canvas at the same time — canvas is a collaboratively edited block, not a private draft. Closing and reopening a canvas Closing the canvas panel doesn't discard your edits as long as you've saved — the block in the conversation updates with your latest saved version. Reopening the same block later (by clicking its edit icon again) picks up where you left off, since it's editing the message's content directly rather than a separate draft. Canvas edits the block that was just generated in the current turn. Opening or saving a previously stored file into canvas isn't supported — canvas has no "open file" action, and its content types are limited to code, tables and Mermaid diagrams. To work with a stored file, use Artifacts instead. Related Use chat Manage artifact buckets and files

title: Use chat
text: Chat is where you talk to models, agents, pipelines, toolkits, and MCP servers in one conversation. Every conversation keeps its own context — nothing is shared between conversations unless you attach the same participant to more than one. Create a conversation Click + Conversation at the top of the sidebar. Pick a model from the selector at the bottom of the composer, or type to search and attach an agent, pipeline, toolkit, or MCP connection that already exists in the project — selected participants appear as chips above the input box. Type your message and send it; the conversation is named automatically from your first message, and you can rename it any time. Organize conversations into folders Click the folder icon next to Conversations at the top of the sidebar to create a folder, then move conversations into it either by dragging one onto the folder, or by right clicking a conversation and choosing Move to . Right click a conversation (or use its options menu) for: Rename , Move to , Playback (step through it turn by turn without sending anything live), Pin/unpin (keeps it at the top of the list), and Delete . Right click a folder for: Rename , Pin/unpin , and Delete — deleting a folder does not delete the conversations in it, they move back to the root list. Visibility in private vs. team projects Conversations and folders are personal — only you can see them. You can still add agents, pipelines, toolkits and MCPs as participants, but you cannot add other users. Folders are visible to every project member. A conversation is visible only to its participants, unless it's explicitly marked public — at which point every project member can see and interact with it. Making a conversation or folder public cannot be undone. In a team project, add a colleague as a conversation participant to collaborate directly — see Add teammates to a conversation. Attach participants Click the + icon in the composer toolbar to open the menu: Modules (the internal tools, listed first), then Agents , Pipelines , Toolkits , and MCPs . Each category lists the items that already exist in the project — pick one to add it as a participant. Not available yet: creating a brand new agent, pipeline, toolkit, or MCP connection from this menu. It only lists existing items to attach. To create one, use Create an agent, Create a pipeline, or Create a toolkit, then come back and attach it. (tracked in 867) You can also type in the message box for the same picker inline, or / to mention a specific tool from a toolkit or MCP that's already a participant (for example /Jira/createIssue ). The search box in each category filters only the participants already loaded on the page — on a project with a very large catalogue, typing a name that hasn't loaded yet finds nothing. Once a participant is attached, click it in the Participants panel to make it active, then send your message. To edit an attached agent, pipeline, or toolkit's configuration without leaving the conversation, see Edit agents, pipelines, toolkits and MCPs from chat. Choose a model and tune settings Click the model selector to pick an LLM. Click the settings icon next to it to adjust generation parameters — the exact fields depend on the model (a reasoning depth control for reasoning models, a creativity/temperature control for standard ones), plus a max completion tokens option and a Steps limit (default 25, range 0–999) that caps how many tool calls a turn can make before the run stops and returns whatever it has. Work with the response Below an assistant message you get Read out (if voice is configured — see Voice), Copy , Regenerate , and Delete . To change your own last message, use its Edit action: the message becomes editable, any attachments stay attached unless you remove them, and Save and apply re sends it and regenerates the answer. Related Attach files to a conversation Use canvas Manage conversation context Elitea MCP Tools (internal tool) Authorize sensitive actions

title: Authorize sensitive actions
text: An administrator can mark specific tools — deleting a repository, running a shell command, dropping a database table — as sensitive. When an agent or pipeline tries to call one, the conversation pauses and shows you an authorization card before the tool runs. You don't configure this yourself; it applies platform wide once an administrator sets it up. What you see The card shows the action as toolkit name.tool name , the exact arguments the tool would run with (with fields like passwords, tokens, and API keys automatically masked), and your organization's policy message explaining why approval is required. Respond Authorize — the tool runs as planned and the conversation continues. Block — the tool is skipped; the agent is told the call was rejected and continues or stops depending on its own logic. Block with comment — same as Block, but you can add a short note explaining what you want instead; that note is passed back to the agent as the reason for the rejection. If the same tool is called again later in the same run, only the first call raises the interrupt — later calls in that batch are auto approved once you've authorized the first one. This works the same way whether the sensitive tool call happens in a plain conversation, inside an agent's own run, or at a toolkit, MCP, code, or LLM node in a pipeline — execution pauses at that exact point and resumes from there once you decide. Configuring which tools are sensitive This is an administrator task, done from the Guardrails section of admin configuration — see Configuration. An admin can mark tools sensitive per toolkit type, per specific toolkit, or for every toolkit with a wildcard, and can customize the organization name and policy message shown on the card. Related Use chat

title: Use public items from chat
text: Published agents from other users (and your own) show up alongside your private ones when you search for a participant, marked with a public badge. You can attach and run them immediately — no setup required. Find and use a public agent Type in the composer and search by name, or open the + menu's Agents category — both list your own agents together with published ones, publicly marked. Select one to attach it as a participant, then click it in the Participants panel to make it active and send your message. You can also browse everything published in the project from the catalog, or open a specific published item directly at its public URL. What you can and can't change Opening a public agent's settings gives you a read only view of its core configuration. You can temporarily change the model, model settings, and variables for your current conversation only — those changes are not saved and reset the next time you start a new conversation with that agent. You cannot edit or save its instructions, toolkit configuration, or other core settings, and you cannot unpublish or delete someone else's agent. If you want to keep a customized version, create your own agent and adapt the public one's approach rather than trying to save over it. Publishing your own The same catalog works both ways — once you've built an agent you're happy with, you can publish it so other project members can find and attach it the same way. See Publish agents and skills for how review and moderation work before your agent shows up as public to others. Public toolkits and pipelines follow the same read only pattern — you can attach and run them, but not edit their saved configuration. Related Use chat Publish an agent or skill

title: Use credentials in a toolkit
text: A credential stores the authentication details a toolkit needs to reach an external service — an API key, a token, or a username and password — so you don't re enter them for every toolkit that talks to the same service. Where credentials live Credentials are scoped to the project (or your personal project) where you create them: Project credentials are shared with the project team. Private credentials are visible only to you. Both kinds appear in a toolkit's credential dropdown when they match the toolkit's type — a Jira toolkit only offers Jira credentials, for example. Create and attach a credential 1. Go to Credentials and select Create credential , or start from a toolkit's configuration form and use its credential dropdown's create option. 2. Pick the credential type that matches your toolkit (for example Jira, GitHub, or Confluence). 3. Fill in the fields the type needs — these vary by service, but commonly include a base URL, a token, or a username and password. 4. Save. If you started from a toolkit form, refresh the credential dropdown to pick up the new credential. Reuse across toolkits Once created, a credential is reusable across every toolkit of the same type in its scope — you don't need a separate credential per toolkit instance. For extra protection on especially sensitive values, you can also route a credential's fields through Secrets. If a credential stops working — a token expired, or the target service changed — edit it once from the Credentials list, and every toolkit that references it picks up the change on its next call. You don't need to open and resave each toolkit individually. Which toolkits need a credential Not every toolkit type needs one: the built in Artifact type reads from your project's own buckets, and a few settings only types (cloud provider integrations, for instance) authenticate a different way. Most toolkits that reach an external system — Jira, GitHub, Confluence, and the rest of the catalogue — need a matching credential before they'll do anything. If a toolkit's credential dropdown is empty, create one from that same dropdown rather than navigating away to the Credentials menu first. Next steps Project vs. private credentials for how the two scopes interact on a shared toolkit. Create a credential for the getting started walkthrough.

title: Automate Jira with Elitea
text: This is a worked example: a Jira Automation rule calls an Elitea agent whenever someone clicks a button on an issue, the agent fetches the issue with its Jira toolkit, reviews it against your instructions, and posts the review back as a comment. Adapt the same pattern to other Jira triggered workflows. Build the review agent 1. Create an agent (or edit an existing one) at /agents/create . 2. Give it instructions that describe the review, for example: "You will receive a Jira issue key as input. Use the Jira toolkit to fetch the issue's details, review it, then post a comment on the same issue summarizing gaps and clarifying questions." 3. Attach a Jira toolkit configured with your Jira instance and a credential that can read and comment on issues — see Use credentials in a toolkit. 4. Save the agent. Set up the API side once Elitea's chat API works against a conversation, not a bare agent call, so you set this up once and reuse it: 1. Create a personal access token for the automation to authenticate with — see Create a personal access token. 2. Create a conversation with your review agent as its participant, and note the conversation's ID and the agent's participant ID within it. 3. Keep both IDs — the automation rule will post every trigger into this same conversation. Configure the Jira Automation rule In Jira, create an Automation rule with a manual trigger (a button on the issue view) and a Send web request action: Method : POST URL : your Elitea instance's message endpoint for the conversation you created ( /api/v2/elitea core/messages/prompt lib/{projectID}/{conversationID} ) Headers : Authorization: Bearer Body : a JSON payload carrying the participant ID and the issue key as the user input, for example using Jira's {{issue.key}} smart value in place of a literal key. The exact request body fields for this endpoint aren't republished here — check the current shape in API usage before wiring the automation rule, since this is a lower level API than the chat UI and its payload can change between releases. Test and troubleshoot Run the automation manually on a test issue first. If nothing happens, check: the personal access token hasn't expired, the conversation and participant IDs are correct, and the Jira credential attached to the toolkit still has permission to comment on the issue. Next steps Use credentials in a toolkit for the Jira credential setup. Webhooks and pipeline triggers for triggering a pipeline instead of an agent.

title: Test toolkit tools
text: Before attaching a toolkit to an agent or a chat, you can run one of its tools directly to confirm the credential works and the tool returns what you expect. Run a test 1. Open a saved toolkit's configuration page (unsaved changes disable testing — save first). 2. Open its Test tools pane. 3. Pick a tool from the list and fill in its arguments. 4. Choose a model if the tool needs one, and run it. 5. Read the result in the transcript alongside the run. Index Data can't be tested here. The Go backend routes it through a separate, asynchronous endpoint owned by the toolkit's Indexes tab; running it from Test tools returns that route's own refusal instead of an actual index run. There's no history of past test runs to come back to — a run's result only exists in this session's transcript (tracked in 868). If you need a persisted record of what a toolkit did, message traces exist as an API — see API usage. What testing verifies A successful run confirms the credential authenticates and the tool's arguments are valid for your instance of the external service — useful before wiring the toolkit into an agent where a failure is harder to diagnose. A failing run typically means a credential problem, a permission problem on the external service, or an argument the service rejects. Choosing which tool to test first If a toolkit exposes many tools, start with the simplest read only one (a list or search operation) rather than something that writes to the external system. That confirms the credential and connection work before you risk a test run creating or modifying real data in Jira, GitHub, or whichever service the toolkit reaches. Once a read tool succeeds, move on to testing the write tools you actually plan to use. Next steps Use credentials in a toolkit if the test fails on authentication. Index and search data with tools for search tools once an index exists.

title: Project vs. private credentials
text: Every credential type a toolkit can use offers the same choice: a project credential or a private credential. The toolkit's credential field states it plainly — project credentials are shared with the project team, private credentials are visible only to you. When to use each Project credentials make sense when a toolkit is shared team infrastructure — a project's GitHub or Jira connection that everyone on the team should be able to use without holding their own token. Private credentials make sense when each teammate should authenticate with their own identity — for example, so that actions a toolkit takes (a Jira comment, a GitHub commit) are attributed to the person who triggered them, not to a shared service account. How it works on a shared toolkit A toolkit instance references one credential at a time. If you want per user attribution on a team shared toolkit, each teammate creates their own private credential of the matching type, then selects it in their own copy of the toolkit's configuration (or in whichever context lets them pick a credential, such as an inline chat editor). The credential scope is a property of the credential itself, not of the toolkit — a toolkit doesn't enforce that everyone use the same kind. In your personal project vs. a team project In your personal project, "project credential" and "private credential" describe the same access — only you can see either one — so the distinction mostly matters once you're working in a team project with other members. There, the choice determines whether a teammate opening the same toolkit sees your credential in the dropdown at all. Deciding which to use A reasonable default: start with a project credential for anything genuinely shared (a bot account, a service integration), and reach for a private credential the moment attribution or personal access scope actually matters — for example when a toolkit posts comments, opens pull requests, or otherwise takes an action that should trace back to an individual rather than the team. Next steps Use credentials in a toolkit for the create and attach flow. Create a credential for the getting started walkthrough.

title: Webhooks and pipeline triggers
text: A pipeline has two unattended ways to start without a person watching a chat: an inbound webhook trigger and a cron schedule. Both live together in the pipeline editor's Triggers & schedules section, and both exist so you can wire a pipeline into an external process — a CI job, an issue tracker automation, a recurring maintenance task — without anyone opening a conversation to kick it off. Pipeline triggers 1. Open a pipeline's configuration and expand Triggers & schedules . 2. Reveal the trigger's secret URL (hidden until you explicitly show it) or rotate it if you suspect it's been exposed. 3. Configure the external system (GitHub, GitLab, or any custom sender) to POST to that URL when the event you want fires. 4. Send the secret as an Authorization: Bearer header where the sender supports it — a token embedded in the URL itself is accepted as a fallback, but it's the less safe option since URLs get written to proxy and browser logs. The same section also configures the cron schedule, and an agent's info panel shows which trigger type (chat message, schedule, or webhook — GitHub, GitLab, or custom) is wired to it. Webhook API Separately from pipeline triggers, each project also has a generic outbound webhook registry — you can register a URL, a list of events, and a secret, and Elitea calls that URL when those events occur. This is a different, newer capability than pipeline triggers, keyed on the project rather than a specific pipeline, and it has no equivalent in the legacy platform. Registering one today means calling the webhook API directly with your personal access token: create an entry with a target URL, the events you want, and a secret Elitea will sign requests with, then verify that signature on your receiving end the same way you would for the pipeline trigger's bearer token. Not available yet: a page to create, list, rotate, or delete these webhooks — use the API directly. (tracked in 876) Next steps Webhooks and triggers reference for the underlying API calls. Pipeline runs for what a triggered run looks like once it starts.

title: Organize agents, pipelines and toolkits
text: As a project accumulates agents, pipelines, toolkits, credentials, and MCP connections, four features keep the catalogue navigable: search, tags, pins, and folders. Search The Agents, Pipelines, Toolkits, Credentials, and MCPs pages each have a search box that matches on name and description, and lets you filter by tag. Type into the box to see matching results grouped by tag and by entity type; select a result to open it directly. Tags Tags are free form labels you attach to an entity to group it by topic, team, or project. Add one from the entity's configuration: 1. Open the entity's configuration. 2. Find the Tags field and start typing. 3. Select a suggested tag or press Enter to create a new one. 4. Save the entity. Tags are shared within a project — anyone with search access can filter by them, which is what makes them useful for grouping work across a team. Pins Pinning keeps an entity at the top of its list, across sessions, so you don't have to scroll or search for something you use constantly. Pin and unpin with a single click from an entity's list row; pinning works for agents, pipelines, toolkits, credentials, and MCPs. Folders Folders group conversations in the chat sidebar — this is new in this platform (the legacy site had no equivalent). Create a folder from the conversation list, then drag conversations into it, or move a conversation into a folder from its context menu. Next steps Use chat for where folders live day to day. Use public items from chat for finding entities other people have published.

title: Index data from a source
text: The overall indexing procedure is the same for every source: configure a credential, pick the embedding model and vector store, set the source's scope fields, then start the run. This page covers the setup each source needs; for the shared procedure and the index lifecycle itself, see Index external data and Use the Indexes tab. Shared setup (do this once per project) 1. In Settings › AI Providers , configure an embedding model and a pgvector vector store connection. 2. Create a toolkit of the source's type (see the tabs below for which credential it needs). 3. Turn on the Index Data tool in the toolkit's configuration. 4. Open the toolkit's Indexes tab and create an index using the source's scope fields. Source specific setup Toolkit type: confluence . Needs a Confluence credential (API token). Scope fields include the space key and optional label/CQL filters. Toolkit type: sharepoint . Needs a SharePoint credential (Azure AD app registration). Scope fields include the site, drive, and folder to index. Toolkit type: ado wiki . Needs an Azure DevOps credential (personal access token). Scope fields include the wiki identifier. Toolkit type: figma . Needs a Figma credential (personal access token). Scope fields include the file or project to index. Built in — no import key or external credential. Indexes files already uploaded to one of your project's artifact buckets. Toolkit type: github . Needs a GitHub credential (personal access token or GitHub App). Scope fields include the repository and branch. Toolkit type: jira . Needs a Jira credential (API token). Scope fields include a JQL query or project filter. Toolkit type: testrail . Needs a TestRail credential (API key). Scope fields include the project or suite. Toolkit type: xray cloud (renamed from the earlier "Xray"). Needs Xray Cloud API credentials (client ID and secret). Toolkit type: zephyr scale , zephyr enterprise , or zephyr essential depending on which Zephyr product you use — each has its own credential shape and its own index capable type. ADO Boards, ADO Plans, ADO Repos, Bitbucket, GitLab, and QTest also carry an indexing tool but had no dedicated legacy page — they follow the same shared procedure using their own credential type. Next steps Use the Indexes tab for the create/reindex/schedule/history workflow. Use credentials in a toolkit for how credentials attach to a toolkit.

title: Index external data
text: Indexing turns content from an external system — a repository, a wiki, a set of issues, or uploaded files — into a searchable store that agents, pipelines, and chat can query with natural language, instead of you browsing the source system by hand. What indexing needs Before you can index anything, three things must be in place: A credential for the target system, attached to the toolkit (not required for the built in Artifact type, which indexes files you've already uploaded). An embedding model configuration, selected at the project level (Settings › AI Providers). A vector store configuration (PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension), also selected at the project level. The Indexes tab only appears on a toolkit whose type declares an indexing tool, and it renders the tab even when the currently running worker can't execute it — in that case it shows the server's own explanation instead of the create index form, rather than hiding the tab. Which toolkit types support indexing 18 toolkit types carry an indexing tool: ADO Boards, ADO Plans, ADO Repos, ADO Wiki, Artifact, Bitbucket, Confluence, Figma, GitHub, GitLab, Jira, QTest, SharePoint, TestRail, XRAY cloud, Zephyr Enterprise, Zephyr Essential, and Zephyr Scale. Any other toolkit type has no Indexes tab at all. Whether an index capable type actually appears as a tile in Create toolkit also depends on which worker your deployment runs — see Use credentials in a toolkit and the toolkit catalogue reference for the worker split. The indexing tools Six tools, available on the toolkit types listed above, do the actual work: Index Data — creates or updates an index for a chosen scope (a repo, a space, a project, and so on). Search Index — runs a semantic search query against a completed index. Stepback Search Index — rewrites a complex query before searching, for better recall on multi part questions. Stepback Summary Index — runs a stepback search and returns a generated summary of the results. Remove Index — deletes an index. List Indexes — lists the indexes a toolkit already has (the Indexes tab shows this list itself, so you rarely need to run this as a tool). For the full setup walkthrough, see Use the Indexes tab. For running search tools from chat or an agent, see Index and search data with tools. Where indexing happens 1. Open a toolkit that supports indexing (for example a GitHub toolkit) and go to its Indexes tab. 2. If no indexes exist yet, use the create index entry point to configure the scope and start a run. 3. Watch the run's status until it reaches Completed or Partially Indexed . 4. Search, re index, schedule, or delete the index from the same tab. Trigger indexing from chat You can also run search tools against an existing index directly from a conversation, by adding the toolkit as a chat participant and enabling its search tools. This is useful for one off questions without opening the toolkit's configuration page — see Use chat. Next steps Use the Indexes tab to create your first index. Index data from a source for source specific setup fields. Schedule re indexing to keep an index current automatically.

title: Index and search data with tools
text: Indexing tools aren't limited to the Indexes tab — once a toolkit has an index, an agent, a pipeline, or a chat conversation with that toolkit attached can call its search tools directly. The tools | Tool | What it does | Where it can run | | | | | | Index Data | Creates or updates an index | Indexes tab only | | Search Index | Direct semantic search over an index | Indexes tab, chat, agents, pipelines, Test tools | | Stepback Search Index | Rewrites the query before searching, for better recall on complex questions | Same as Search Index | | Stepback Summary Index | Runs a stepback search and returns a generated summary | Same as Search Index | | Remove Index | Deletes an index | Indexes tab only | | List Indexes | Lists a toolkit's indexes | Rarely needed — the Indexes tab already lists them | Index Data can't be tested from the Test tools pane. The Go backend routes indexing through a separate, asynchronous endpoint owned by the Indexes tab. If you press Run on Index Data from a toolkit's Test tools pane, you get that route's own refusal rather than a result — use the Indexes tab to actually create or update an index. Search from chat or an agent 1. Add the indexed toolkit as a participant in a conversation, or attach it to an agent. 2. Make sure the search tool you want (Search Index, Stepback Search Index, or Stepback Summary Index) is turned on in the toolkit's configuration. 3. Ask a question in natural language. The toolkit runs the search tool against the index and returns matching content — or, with Stepback Summary Index, a generated summary of it. Search from the Indexes tab You can also run these search tools directly from an index's own page, without going through chat — useful for quickly checking what an index actually returns before wiring it into an agent. Vector store and embeddings Search quality depends on the same two project level configurations indexing itself needs: an embedding model (to turn your query into a vector) and a pgvector vector store configuration (where the vectors are stored and compared). See Index external data for how to set these up. Next steps Use the Indexes tab to create an index in the first place. Schedule re indexing to keep results current.

title: Schedule re-indexing
text: Scheduled reindexing keeps an index synchronized with its source automatically, instead of you having to reindex by hand every time the underlying content changes. Before you schedule The index must already exist and be in a usable state — Completed or Partially Indexed . An index in Failed or Stopped state needs a successful reindex first. If the toolkit requires credentials for the scheduled run, you'll need one available: private credentials in a personal project, project credentials in a team project. Set a schedule 1. Open the index's page from the toolkit's Indexes tab. 2. In the Schedule section, select + Schedule if none exists yet, or the edit icon on an existing schedule. 3. Choose a cron expression — either with the visual builder or by typing one directly (format: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week). 4. If the toolkit needs credentials for the scheduled run, pick one from the dropdown. 5. Save. The schedule shows its next run time, and you can turn it on or off later without losing the configured expression. Each schedule belongs to one index. You can turn it off temporarily with the toggle, or delete it with the edit panel's delete icon, without affecting the index's data. Notifications and history A scheduled reindex raises a notification when it completes, just like a manual one — see Notifications. Scheduled runs also appear in the index's history alongside manual reindexes, so you can confirm a schedule actually ran. Next steps Use the Indexes tab for the full index lifecycle. Index data from a source for source specific setup. This page could not verify from source whether a scheduled reindex only pulls changes since the last run or reprocesses the source in full each time — check your deployment's behavior before relying on a tight schedule for a large, frequently changing source.

title: Use the Indexes tab
text: Every toolkit type that supports indexing shows an Indexes tab next to its Configuration tab. This page walks through the full lifecycle: create, monitor, reindex, schedule, and review history. Before you start, confirm your project has an embedding model and a pgvector vector store configuration (Settings › AI Providers), and that the toolkit's Index Data tool is turned on. Without these, the tab shows an explanation instead of the create index form — see Index external data. Create an index 1. Open a toolkit that supports indexing and switch to its Indexes tab. 2. Start a new index. Give it a unique name (it can't be changed later) and set the toolkit specific scope fields — for example a repository and branch for GitHub, or a space key for Confluence. See Index data from a source for the fields each source needs. 3. Optionally turn off "skip unsupported extensions" if you want files with uncommon extensions indexed as plain text instead of skipped. 4. Start the run and watch its progress. The index reaches Completed when everything indexed cleanly, or Partially Indexed when some files were skipped (both states are fully searchable). An index in Failed or Stopped state did not complete and needs another run before it's usable. Manage an existing index Opening an index from its card gives you a Configuration view (the index's own settings — everything except its name is editable) and a history view. From there you can: Reindex — pick up new and changed content from the source. Unchanged files aren't reprocessed; the previous working index stays searchable until the new run finishes successfully. Schedule — see Schedule re indexing. Delete — permanently remove the index and its data. Only available when the toolkit's Remove Index tool is turned on. Review index history The index's history view lists every past run — the initial index, manual reindexes, and scheduled reindexes — in order, with status and file counts for each. Use it to confirm a scheduled reindex actually ran, or to see when an index last failed. Notifications Indexing operations (initial runs and reindexes) raise a notification when they finish, whether they succeed, partially succeed, or fail. See Notifications for how to review these. Next steps Index and search data with tools to run search against a completed index from chat or an agent. Schedule re indexing to keep an index current automatically.

title: Use the flow editor
text: The flow editor is the visual workspace for building a pipeline: a canvas you arrange nodes on, connected by the edges the pipeline follows at runtime. Open the flow editor Open Pipelines , then an existing pipeline or a new one, and select Flow in its Configuration tab (next to YAML ). Both views describe the same pipeline and stay in sync — a change in one shows up in the other. Add and connect a node Click the + button on the canvas to open the Add node menu. Choose from the nine types the runtime executes: Agent, Decision, HITL, LLM, MCP, Printer, Router, State modifier, Toolkit. See Pipeline node types for what each does. Click the new node to open its configuration panel and set its fields (model, toolkit, routing condition, and so on, depending on the type). Drag from one node's connection point to the next to create an edge. You can also start a connection and drop it on empty canvas to add a new node in the same step. Code and Custom node types are not offered in the Add node menu — the runtime has no execution logic for either. A pipeline authored before this restriction that still contains one keeps displaying it, but you cannot add a new one. Canvas controls The left side toolbar zooms in and out, fits the whole pipeline to view, locks the canvas against accidental edits, collapses or expands all node cards at once, and auto arranges the layout. Guides and references Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Edit a pipeline as YAML Pipeline node types

title: Control-flow nodes: decision, router and state
text: Control flow nodes decide what happens next, or reshape the pipeline's state without calling an external service. Router Evaluates a template condition (Jinja style) against the pipeline's state and picks one of several named routes, with a default fallback if nothing matches. | Field | What it does | | | | | Condition | A template that resolves to one of your route names — for example, branching on whether a state variable contains "approved" | | Routes | The node IDs the condition can resolve to; route names must exactly match a node ID, case sensitively | | Default output | Where to go if the condition resolves to nothing recognized | Router is fast and deterministic — no model call — best when the branching logic is an explicit rule. Decision Uses an LLM to pick a route based on a natural language description, instead of a template rule. Best for routing that depends on interpreting meaning rather than matching a fixed pattern. | Field | What it does | | | | | Description | Plain language instructions telling the model how to choose between routes | | Decision outputs | The node IDs the model can choose from | | Default output | Fallback route if the model can't decide confidently | Decision nodes are slower than Router (they make a model call) and cannot connect directly to another Decision node — put a Router, LLM, or Toolkit node between two decisions if you need a second one in sequence. State modifier Reshapes the pipeline's state without calling a model or a tool: combine values, format text, do simple arithmetic, or clear out variables you no longer need. | Field | What it does | | | | | Template | A Jinja style template referencing input variables — for example, Hello, {{ user name }}! | | Input | The state variables the template is allowed to read | | Output | Where the rendered result is written | | Variables to clean | Optional list of variables to reset afterward (strings to "" , lists to [] , numbers to 0 ) | Guides and references Pipeline node types Interaction nodes: HITL and printer Execution nodes: LLM, agent, toolkit, MCP Pipeline structure: entry point, state and connections

title: Execution nodes: LLM, agent, toolkit and MCP
text: Execution nodes are where a pipeline does its work — calling a model, delegating to an agent, or running a specific tool with known parameters. LLM Calls a model directly with a system message and a task, without wrapping it in a full agent. Useful when you know exactly what you want asked and don't need an agent's own toolkits or persona. | Field | What it does | | | | | System | Fixed text, a template, or a state variable — sets the model's role/behavior | | Task | The request sent to the model, same three input types | | Chat history | What prior conversation context (if any) to include | | Input / Output | Which state variables feed in, and which are populated from the response | | Toolkits | Toolkits or MCPs the model can call as tools during this step | | Structured output | When enabled, the response is parsed into your named output variables instead of dropped into messages as free text | Agent Delegates the step to an agent you've already added to the pipeline (Pipeline Configuration › Toolkits), reusing its instructions, model and attached toolkits instead of reconfiguring an LLM call from scratch. | Field | What it does | | | | | Agent | Which added agent runs this step | | Task | The instruction sent to the agent — fixed, templated, or from state | | Input / Output | Same pattern as the LLM node | | Custom variables | Values for any custom variables the agent's own configuration defines | Toolkit Calls one specific tool from a toolkit already attached to the pipeline, with parameters mapped directly from state — no LLM call, fast and deterministic. | Field | What it does | | | | | Toolkit / Tool | Which attached toolkit, and which of its tools to run | | Input mapping | Maps each of the tool's parameters to a fixed value, a template, or a state variable | | Output | Where the tool's result is written | MCP Calls one tool from a connected MCP server, the same way the Toolkit node calls a toolkit tool — direct parameter mapping, no LLM step. MCP nodes only reach MCP servers; for an Elitea toolkit's own tools, use the Toolkit node instead. | Field | What it does | | | | | MCP server / Tool | Which connected MCP server and which of its tools | | Input mapping | Maps the tool's parameters, same as the Toolkit node | | Structured output | Parse the tool's result into named state variables instead of messages | Guides and references Pipeline node types Interaction nodes: HITL and printer Control flow nodes: decision, router and state Use credentials

title: Interaction nodes: human-in-the-loop and printer
text: Interaction nodes are where a pipeline talks to a person, either to ask for a decision or to hand back a formatted result. Human in the loop (HITL) A HITL node pauses the pipeline and waits for a person to respond with one of three actions, each routable to a different next node: | Action | Typical use | | | | | Approve | Continue down the main path | | Edit | Send a modified value back into the pipeline before continuing — this needs a state key configured to receive the edit | | Reject | Stop or divert to a different path | Connect each action to whichever node should run next; an action with no route configured has nowhere to go. A HITL node is how you build an explicit approval step into a pipeline's own logic — distinct from the guardrail confirmation prompt that can appear in chat before a sensitive tool call, which is triggered by admin configuration rather than a node you place yourself. See Require confirmation for sensitive actions for that related flow. Printer A Printer node formats a final message and writes it to the pipeline's output — typically the last node before END in a path that should show something back to the user. It takes the content you want printed (which can reference earlier state) and stores it in the reserved printer output state key. Because printer output is a reserved state key, don't reuse it for anything else in the same pipeline — a later node that overwrites it silently replaces whatever the Printer node produced. See Pipeline structure for the full list of reserved keys. Guides and references Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Execution nodes: LLM, agent, toolkit and MCP Control flow nodes: decision, router and state

title: Pipeline node types
text: The flow editor lets you drop more node types onto the canvas than the runtime actually executes. Nine types are admitted by the compiler; the rest render for reference but do nothing when the pipeline runs. The nine runtime admitted types | Category | Node types | See | | | | | | Interaction | Human in the loop (HITL), Printer | Interaction nodes | | Execution | LLM, Agent, Toolkit, MCP | Execution nodes | | Control flow | Decision, Router, State modifier | Control flow nodes | Deprecated node types The Add node menu only ever offers the nine types above — these older types can't be added to a new pipeline. If a pipeline built before this platform still has one, it renders read only on the canvas, but the compiler has no execution arm for it, so it doesn't run: Tool , Function , Pipeline , Condition , Loop , Loop from tool . If you're rebuilding a pipeline that still has one of these, replace it with the closest supported type: a Tool node becomes a Toolkit node, a Condition node becomes a Decision or Router node, and a Loop is restructured as a Router cycling back to an earlier node with an exit condition. There is no automatic migration — each one is a manual edit. A couple of other node shaped entries are sentinels rather than real node types: END marks where a path terminates (see Pipeline structure), and ghost /the default type are placeholders the editor uses internally. Two types that render but never run code and custom nodes can be added to a pipeline and configured in the flow editor, but the compiler has no execution arm for either one — they're accepted by the editor for future use, not by the runtime today. Don't build a pipeline that depends on one of these actually running; use an equivalent from the nine admitted types instead (a Toolkit node for custom logic that calls out to a service, for example).

title: Pipelines overview
text: A pipeline is a visual workflow: a sequence of connected nodes that execute in order, carrying a shared state between them. Where an agent has a single conversational loop, a pipeline lets you compose multiple steps — calling a toolkit, asking an LLM, branching on a decision, pausing for human approval — into one repeatable process. How a pipeline runs 1. Execution starts at the pipeline's designated entry point. 2. Each node performs its action and writes results into the pipeline's shared state. 3. The pipeline follows the connection from the current node to the next, based on the node's own routing (a plain edge, or a decision/router node's branch). 4. Execution ends when a transition reaches END . What a pipeline can use The flow editor's Add node menu only offers node types the runtime actually executes. Nine node types are admitted : decision , agent , toolkit , mcp , hitl , llm , printer , router , state modifier . Six older types — tool , pipeline , function , loop , loop from tool , condition — are deprecated: they still render if an older pipeline already contains them, but you cannot add new ones, and they carry a "Deprecated" badge in the editor. See Pipeline node types for the full comparison, and Pipeline structure for entry points, state and connections. For the full reference table, see Pipeline node reference. When to use a pipeline instead of an agent Reach for a pipeline when you need a defined, repeatable sequence of steps — gather input, call a toolkit, branch on the result, get human approval, produce an output — rather than an open ended conversation. Use an agent when the interaction should stay conversational and let the model decide what to do next. The two compose: a pipeline can include an agent node, and an agent can be attached to a chat conversation the same way a pipeline can. Guides and references Use the flow editor Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Pipeline node types View pipeline runs

title: View pipeline runs
text: When you run a pipeline, the flow editor shows progress directly on the canvas: nodes the run has reached pick up a status, and a run state indicator lets you open a step by step view of what happened. Run the pipeline (from its Configuration tab, or by using it in a conversation). As execution proceeds, nodes on the canvas update to show whether they're pending, running, done, or failed. Click the run state indicator to open a dialog with a stepper across every step the run has taken so far. Select a step to see the pipeline's state before and after it ran. From the same dialog, you can stop a run in progress. This page could not confirm from source whether a run's timeline stays inspectable after you navigate away and back, or only while the run view stays open — verify locally before relying on it for after the fact debugging. There is no separate "run history" list page for pipelines (tracked in 868); see Import and export entities if you need a durable record of a specific configuration. Reading a step's state Each step in the timeline shows the pipeline's state as it was immediately before and immediately after that node ran. This is the most direct way to see what a Decision or Router node actually branched on, or what an LLM node's raw output was before a later node reshaped it — useful for working out why a pipeline took the path it did, or why it stopped where it did. A step that fails is marked with its own error status in the timeline, alongside the state at that point — checking the state there is usually the fastest way to tell whether the problem was bad input, a missing credential, or a node reading a state key that was never set. Guides and references Use the flow editor Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Pipeline node types

title: Pipeline structure: state, entry point and connections
text: A pipeline is a graph of nodes connected by transitions, with one starting point and one shared state object that every node can read and write. State: the pipeline's memory State is a structured object carried from node to node. Two states exist on every pipeline automatically: | State | Type | Holds | | | | | | input | string | The most recent user message | | messages | list | The full conversation history | Both are built in, but neither is reserved — you can read or write them like any other state key, and a new pipeline starts with them present but disabled until you turn them on for a node that needs them. Beyond those two, a pipeline has a fixed set of reserved keys the runtime manages itself — things like session id , thread id , output , result , hitl decisions , hitl interrupt , parallel tasks , and a family of internal resume markers. You can read them from a node, but avoid naming a custom state the same as one of these — the runtime will overwrite it with its own value. elitea hitl resume v1 , elitea tool resume v1 , elitea llm tool resume v1 , elitea pipeline node event scope v1 , elitea application task v1 , elitea application messages v1 , elitea application result v1 , elitea subgraph result v1 , output , result , router output , elitea response , printer output , state types , context info , hitl decisions , hitl interrupt , parallel tasks , pipeline blocked , session id , thread id , execution finished , chat history Add a custom state from the flow editor's States panel (next to the + button for adding nodes), or define it directly in YAML mode. Entry point Every pipeline has exactly one entry point — the node that runs first. Set it from a node's options menu ( Make entrypoint ), or in YAML with entry point: . A router node cannot be the entry point — it needs input from an earlier node to decide where to go. Setting a new entry point replaces the previous one; only one node holds it at a time. Node ports and connections Every node has one input port (top) and one output port (bottom). Most node types allow only a single outgoing connection; router and decision nodes are the exception — they can fan out to multiple targets, one of which is a labeled default/fallback path. Node names (ids) are restricted to letters, digits, , . , : and , up to 128 bytes. Ending a run END isn't a real node — it's a special connection target that stops execution. Drag a connector to the canvas and choose END , or set transition: END in YAML. Every path through the pipeline should eventually reach it; a path that never terminates can leave a run hanging.

title: Edit a pipeline as YAML
text: Alongside the flow editor, a pipeline's Configuration tab has a YAML view: a code editor over the same document the flow editor draws. A change in either view is reflected in the other — neither is a snapshot of the other. Schema Every pipeline document has three required top level sections: entry point names the node id execution starts from. state declares the pipeline's variables — each with a type and, optionally, a default value: input and messages are built in — the editor seeds them automatically and they don't need an initial value. Beyond those two, a state key cannot use one of the runtime's reserved names ( output , session id , chat history , and others the compiler uses internally) — see Pipeline structure for the full list. nodes is the array of node definitions — each entry names a node id (matching ^[A Za z0 9 .: ]+$ , at most 128 bytes) and a type from the nine the runtime admits. When to use YAML instead of Flow The YAML view is useful for copying a pipeline definition out for review or version control, editing many nodes at once, or working faster once you know the schema. For visually laying out nodes and connections, use the flow editor instead — the two views edit the same document, so switch freely. A minimal example This isn't a runnable pipeline on its own — it's meant to show the shape: an entry point, a state block, and a nodes array where each entry has an id and a type . A real pipeline also wires up each node's configuration (prompt, model, routing conditions), its connections to the next node, and a path into the reserved END sentinel to terminate — see Pipeline node types for why END isn't a node type you configure like the others. Guides and references Use the flow editor Pipeline structure: entry point, states and connections Pipeline node types

title: Elitea Docs
text: Elitea brings chat, agents, pipelines, toolkits, and platform administration into one workspace. These docs cover what the platform does today, how to set it up, and how to use each part of it. Concepts, the main menus, and personal and project settings. Install the platform and send your first chat message. Task by task instructions for chat, pipelines, indexing, and more. Toolkits, MCP servers, and third party API access. Console for users, roles, authentication, budgets, and branding. Where to start New to Elitea? Read Overview of the Elitea platform, then Key concepts. Setting up a fresh deployment? Follow Install, then Configure an AI provider. Ready to chat? Go straight to Chat quick start. Connecting an external tool? See Connect toolkits quick start or the toolkit catalogue. Administering a deployment? Start at Admin overview. Something not working? Check Troubleshooting or the FAQs.

title: Inventory
text: Inventory ingests one or more source repositories into a knowledge graph — files, functions, types and the relations between them — that you can filter, browse and ask questions of. Like Wikis, it lives at its own Inventory area, addressed by the Inventory toolkit that built the graph. Prerequisites An Inventory toolkit with at least one source added. A source toolkit of an allowed type — by default GitHub or ADO Repos (a deployment can widen this with ELITEA INVENTORY SOURCE TYPES ; GitLab and Bitbucket are not supported as sources even when connected as toolkits elsewhere). An llm model set on the Inventory toolkit — ingestion is refused without one. Build a knowledge graph If the project has none yet, add one — the Inventory area prompts you to when it finds none for the project. Under Sources , add a source toolkit (GitHub or ADO Repos, unless the deployment allows more) and its branch. Select Run ingestion . Progress shows per source: Pending, Ingesting…, Done, or Error. You can Stop ingestion on a source that's running. Browse the graph Filter entities by source, type and layer, and search by name. Select an entity to see its file location and its relations — incoming and outgoing edges to other entities. A source removed from the toolkit but still represented in the graph shows as "No longer configured — its entities are still in the graph," rather than disappearing silently. Ask about the inventory Select Ask this inventory to open a question panel over the graph. Answers name the entities they came from, rather than answering from general knowledge. Statistics and maintenance The Stats view breaks the graph down by layer and entity type, and reports cache size and cached graph count. Maintenance normalizes type name variations (for example "Feature" vs. "feature") and rebuilds the name, type, file and source indices. Common issues Inventory runs on the deployment's engine sidecar, not the Rust/Python agent worker — ingestion and browsing work the same regardless of which worker your deployment runs for agents and toolkits. "This toolkit configures no LLM model, so ingestion is refused" means you must set llm model in the Inventory toolkit's settings before Run ingestion will do anything. If the ingestion status can't be read, the per source states shown are stale, not necessarily current — re check after a refresh rather than assuming a source is still Pending.

title: Wikis (DeepWiki)
text: DeepWiki turns a code repository — or a folder of files in an artifact bucket — into browsable documentation: a page tree, diagrams, and a chat you can ask questions of. It lives at its own Wikis area, addressed by the wiki toolkit that generated it, rather than under Toolkits. DeepWiki needs the deployment's engine image tag and ELITEA DEEPWIKI ENABLED . A deployment on the default image lists and reads existing wikis but refuses every generation request. Prerequisites A wiki toolkit pointed at a source: a Repository (via a GitHub, GitLab or ADO Repos toolkit you've already connected), an Artifact folder , or a Bucket . An llm model and embedding model set on the toolkit, or a project default for both — generation and wiki chat fall back to the project's default model when the toolkit sets none, and refuse outright if the project has none either. Generate a wiki If the project has none yet, add one — the Wikis area prompts you to when it finds none for the project. Under the toolkit's own settings, set the wiki source: a repository toolkit to clone, an artifact folder, or a bucket. Optionally set a folder prefix to scope a bucket or artifact source. Select Generate wiki . Choose a planner mode ( Agentic or Clustering ) and whether to Skip tests , then confirm. Generation can take several minutes and runs one at a time per slot — if all slots are busy, wait or stop another run first. Browse and edit Once generated, browse the page tree, open Edit page to hand correct a page (diagrams that fail to render offer a one click fix you can accept or discard), and use Delete wiki to remove generated pages. Ask about the wiki Select Ask about this repository to open the chat drawer. You can attach specific wiki pages as context for your question — this attaches page content, not an uploaded file. Wiki chat history is read only once a session ends — you can review past turns but not continue a conversation ("attachments" here means attaching wiki pages, not uploading a file; tracked in 873). Common issues DeepWiki runs on the deployment's engine sidecar, not the Rust/Python agent worker — generation and wiki chat work the same regardless of which worker your deployment runs for agents and toolkits. "No embedding model is set" or "No llm model is set" warnings mean generation or chat will use the project's default model for that role — and refuse outright if the project has none.

title: Make toolkit tools available by MCP
text: Agents and pipelines reach MCP clients through a tag, but toolkit tools reach them through a per toolkit checkbox: Make tools available by MCP , in the toolkit editor's Tools section. Only the tools you've selected on a flagged toolkit are published; nothing is exposed by default. Expose a toolkit's tools Open an existing toolkit (or create one — see the toolkit's own page under Toolkits), and go to its Tools tab. Choose which of the toolkit's tools should be callable at all (the same selection agents and pipelines use). Check Make tools available by MCP . Elitea publishes one MCP tool per selected tool, named (for example github create issue ). Select Save . The client's next tools/list call picks up the change — reconnect the client if it caches the tool list for the session. How a call runs A tools/call for a published toolkit tool dispatches through the same run path chat uses — with idempotency and polling for the worker's result — not a stub. It still needs the toolkit's own prerequisites: the right worker for that toolkit type, and a working credential. Common issues This only controls MCP exposure — the toolkit still needs to work in ordinary use (the right worker, a valid credential) before its tools will succeed when an MCP client calls them; see the toolkit's own page for that.

title: Elitea MCP server
text: Elitea is itself an MCP server: any client that speaks the Model Context Protocol can call your tagged agents, pipelines and toolkit tools as MCP tools. The transport is streamable HTTP — a single POST endpoint that answers initialize , tools/list and tools/call . There is no SSE stream and no stdio server: a GET on the endpoint answers "The server does not offer an SSE stream at this endpoint." Prerequisites Your project's MCP endpoint: https:// /app/ /mcp . A personal access token, sent as Authorization: Bearer . The server authenticates every request as that token's owner and scopes results to projects they belong to. At least one agent or pipeline tagged mcp , or a toolkit with tools marked "available by MCP" (see Make tools available by MCP) — otherwise tools/list returns an empty, but correct, list. Tag an agent or pipeline for MCP Open the agent or pipeline you want to expose. Add the tag mcp to it. Elitea exposes one tool per tagged agent/pipeline, taking a single free form task string as input. If the agent has several tagged versions, the newest tagged one is the one served — not necessarily the version marked "latest" in the UI. Retag or delete older tagged versions if you need a specific one served. Connect a client Add a server entry to .vscode/mcp.json (workspace) or your user mcp.json (global): Reload the MCP server list, then select tools from your Elitea project in Copilot Chat's Agent mode. Common issues Calling a toolkit tool through this MCP server needs the Python worker's toolkit dispatch — on the Rust worker (Helm's default), a toolkit tool call answers a protocol error instead of a result. Agent and pipeline tools tagged mcp run the same way on either worker. Two agents that sanitize to the same tool name collapse into one entry in tools/list — whichever the database returns first wins, silently. Give MCP tagged agents and pipelines unique names. A client that opens a GET (SSE) connection to the endpoint gets a 405, not a stream. If your client only supports the older SSE transport, it can't connect here — use a client that speaks streamable HTTP.

title: Pre-built MCP servers
text: An admin can curate a catalogue of MCP servers that every project sees as ready made toolkit tiles, so project members don't each have to look up a URL and register their own OAuth client. This replaces what the legacy docs called "EPAM MCPs" — the mechanism is now vendor neutral; an admin can add any MCP server here, not a fixed list. Add a server to the catalogue As an admin, open Configuration in the admin console and go to the MCP servers section. Select Add MCP server . Give it a display name (its catalogue key is derived from the name, or fixed once other projects reference it) and the server's base URL. If the server needs OAuth and doesn't support Dynamic Client Registration, enter the OAuth client ID and client secret . The secret is sealed into the platform vault immediately — no endpoint ever returns it again, including this form on a later edit. Check Offer this server to projects , then Save . Project members now see it as a tile, the same as a hand added Remote MCP. Common issues A catalogued server is a built in Elitea type, not part of the SDK worker capability catalogue. Both the Rust and Python workers can call its tools — only HTTP based servers can be catalogued in the first place, and that is the only transport either worker's MCP client needs. Removing a catalogued server deletes its stored client secret permanently. To stop offering a server without losing the secret, edit it and clear Offer this server to projects instead of deleting it. Stdio transport MCP servers are refused here — only HTTP based remote servers can be catalogued.

title: Remote MCP
text: Remote MCP is the other direction from the Elitea MCP server: instead of exposing Elitea's tools to an external client, a Remote MCP toolkit lets an Elitea agent or pipeline call tools hosted on someone else's MCP server. It's listed as Remote MCP in the toolkit type picker; there is no local or stdio MCP client — only this HTTP connection. Prerequisites The remote server's URL. If the server requires OAuth: either nothing further (if it supports Dynamic Client Registration) or a pre registered OAuth client ID and secret from that server's own admin console. Connect a remote MCP server In the left navigation, open Toolkits , then select New , and choose Remote MCP . Enter the remote server's URL and save. If the server requires OAuth, Elitea opens an authorization dialog — automatically, either now or the first time an agent tries to call one of its tools. Servers that support Dynamic Client Registration need nothing from you beyond clicking Authorize ; a server that doesn't asks for a Client ID and Client Secret first. The flow uses PKCE or OIDC depending on what the server advertises, and you can choose to remember the credentials for the session. Once authorized, Elitea calls the remote server's tools/list and shows the tools it offers. Attach the toolkit to an agent or pipeline the same way as any other toolkit. Common issues Remote MCP is a built in Elitea type, not part of the SDK worker capability catalogue. Both the Rust and Python workers can call a Remote MCP toolkit's tools — the Rust worker's MCP client only speaks streamable HTTP, which is the only transport a remote server can use here anyway. Authorization can happen mid conversation: if a tool call fails because the session isn't authorized yet, Elitea shows the same authorization dialog from chat. If you're testing behind a proxy or a non default host, make sure that path is reachable at the same origin the browser used to start the flow.

title: API usage
text: Everything the web app does goes through the same REST API you can call directly — from a script, a Power Automate flow, or any HTTP client that can send a bearer token. Authenticate Open Settings › Personal tokens and create a token. Copy it immediately — it's shown once. Add an Authorization: Bearer header. A pylon compatibility alternative, X API Key: , is also accepted. Most endpoints take a project id in the path. A token can only act on projects its owner belongs to. Endpoint layout REST endpoints live under /api/v2/... — the same paths the web app calls. Interactive API documentation (OpenAPI/Swagger UI) is served at /api/docs , with the raw spec at /api/openapi.yaml and /api/openapi.json . Both are public — no token needed to read the spec. The MCP server is at /app/{projectID}/mcp (see Elitea MCP server) — the same bearer token authenticates it. SCIM provisioning, for identity providers that push users and groups, is at /api/v2/scim/v2 . It's configured per identity provider under Authentication, not by a personal token. Call the API from Power Automate (or any HTTP client) In your flow, add a generic HTTP (or "HTTP with Azure AD" if you prefer a service account) action. Point it at the /api/v2/... path for the operation you need — check /api/docs for the exact path, parameters and body shape. Set the header to Bearer , stored as a secret in your flow, not inline in plain text. Common issues A token only reaches projects its owner belongs to — a 403 on an otherwise correct call usually means the token owner isn't a member of the project id in the path, not a malformed request. Webhooks (inbound triggers for pipelines) are API only: there is no elitea web page to create, list, rotate or delete one (tracked in 876). The agent's own info panel shows a trigger's URL once one exists.

title: Custom
text: Custom isn't a vendor integration — it's a fallback editor. Every toolkit type normally gets a typed form built from its schema, but Custom always appears at the bottom of the type picker as a generic JSON settings editor you can point at any type. Use it when a type has no typed form yet, or when you need to set a field the form doesn't expose. Custom is added by the web client itself and has no entry in the toolkit type catalogue — there's no fixed tool list or worker verdict to report, because it isn't a type on its own. It edits the settings of whatever underlying toolkit type you choose. Prerequisites The toolkit type key you want to configure (for example github or jira ) and the field names its schema expects — check that type's own page in this catalogue, or the type's settings in the create form first. Any credential the underlying type needs, created the normal way under Credentials. Configure a toolkit as raw JSON In the left navigation, open Toolkits , then select New . Custom is listed at the end of the type picker, outside the category filters. The editor is a JSON text area with syntax highlighting and linting. Enter the type and settings fields the underlying toolkit type expects. Name the toolkit and select Create . Elitea validates the JSON but does not re check it against the target type's schema beyond basic parsing — a field name typo won't be caught here. Available tools There's no fixed tool list — the tools exposed are whatever the underlying toolkit type provides once its settings are valid. Common issues A malformed or incomplete settings object saves without error but fails at call time, not at save time. Prefer the type's own dedicated form when one is available, and reach for Custom only for the fields it's missing.

title: Agents
text: An agent combines instructions, a model, and optional toolkits and skills into a reusable assistant. This page covers the Agents menu end to end; for the underlying concept, see What is an agent. Create an agent Select + Agent in the sidebar. Name and Description are required; Instructions define the agent's behavior. Tags, a welcome message, and up to four conversation starters are optional. Saving creates the agent's first ("latest") version and opens its full configuration page: a form on the left, a live test chat on the right. Select Build with AI on a new agent, or Edit with AI on a saved one, to describe what you want in plain language and review a generated draft — name, description, instructions, welcome message, starters, and suggested toolkits — before applying it. Attach toolkits, agents, MCPs, and pipelines In the Tools section, use the +Toolkit , +MCP , +Agent , and +Pipeline buttons to attach existing resources; each opens a searchable picker with a Create new option that takes you to that resource's own creation form. Changes save automatically. If an attached toolkit uses shared credentials that require your own private copy, a Credential setup required banner appears on its card — select Create a credential to add the matching private credential. Skills Attach up to five skills per agent version from the Skills section. Each attached skill uses its base version by default; select the version name on the card to switch to a different one. The Skills section is hidden when the Public project is selected. Modules Built in modules — attachments, image creation, data analysis, planner, smart tools selection, swarm mode, and the platform's own MCP tools — turn on in Tools › Modules . All except attachments require the Python worker; see Internal tools. Instructions, variables, and mentions Type / in Instructions to mention a toolkit, MCP, agent, or pipeline already attached to the agent, and ~ to mention an attached skill. A {{variable name}} placeholder in Instructions automatically adds a matching input field to the Variables section. Editor notes A free text Editor Notes field records internal context about the current version — it is never sent to the model or used during execution. Test the agent The embedded chat panel on the right lets you send messages, pick a model and its settings (Reasoning for reasoning models, Creativity for standard ones, Max Completion Tokens), and iterate without leaving the page. When context management is on for the project, a Context Budget widget appears above the panel after the first message. Versions Selecting Save again updates the current version. Use Save As Version to branch off a named version instead — version names must be 48 characters or fewer, without spaces or underscores. From any version you can Delete , Execute , or switch versions from the version dropdown. See Entity versioning. Publish, export, import, and fork Publish a draft version through a guided wizard with automated AI validation, making it visible in Catalog. See Agent publishing. Export downloads the selected version as a single .md file, or a .zip if it references nested agents. Import an exported file from the Agents dashboard toolbar. Fork copies the selected version into another project you choose. See Import/export and Forking for full detail; toolkit credentials must be reconfigured manually after either operation. Evaluation A saved agent's editor includes an Evaluation tab to define what "good" looks like for that agent, run it against test cases, and see how it scored. Define scoring dimensions — the criteria a run is judged against, such as accuracy or tone — building up a reusable set of judging criteria before running anything. Create a dataset of test cases: inputs paired with what you expect the agent to do with them. A run executes against a dataset. Start a run against a dataset and your dimensions. Runs poll for progress while this tab stays open — leaving it pauses polling until you return — and produce a scorecard with one score per dimension per case when they finish. Best practices Be specific about the agent's goal, scope, and constraints; give examples where useful. Attach only the toolkits and tools the agent actually needs. Branch a version before a change you might need to roll back from. Run the agent through its conversation starters and a few edge cases before you publish it. Troubleshooting Check the selected model and its settings, and confirm any attached toolkits are configured correctly. Confirm you have publishing permission and that all required fields are complete; review the AI validation result for blocking issues. Save the agent first — Skills can only be attached to a saved version — or check whether the five skill limit has been reached.
